div.head: LADIES' LETTER
div.p: LADIES' LETTER

&TY DEAR NELLIE, As the summer passes by the decoration of our headgear is becoming, if anything, more prolific than ever before. Hats of light material are still very much to the fore. A white satin plait is becoming a prominent feature in the season's millinery, but, generally speaking, plain straw holds the palm. I hear that the largest straw hat ever made has been shipped to Australia. It was not, I may parenthetically remark, made for a lady to wear because the headgear is 6 feet 6 inches across the brim and contains about 200 yards of one-inch jumbo plait. I will now speak of the trimming of ladies' hats generally. Flowers still hold the predominance, and one I saw the other day was arranged with poppies and wheat. I wondered if the wearer intended to be seasonable, tor the crop would have done honour to many a field just now.

One of the prettiest shirts I have yet seen is made with V-shaped, of fish-fin pattern, tucks in front, separated by a small box pleat, studded with the very tiny new buttons of cut steel, gold, or enamel. The small flat turquoise button set in a rim of out steel can be used for this purpose. Coloured out crystal barrel buttons are used for the ooatlets now so much worn. There are a lob of pretty blouses about now and many of them are of very tasteful design. One, a friend of mine was wearing, had such a pretty bow at the throat. The blouse was of blue silk muslin with a very full fron t.

There are many good materials of which boating costumes can be made and one of the best I think in foulard. Of course they must have a sailor collar. Anything to be worn afloat must have this decora• tion. I saw one the other day on a lady in a boat on a river not far from where I was visiting. The inside on the chest was filled with a front of blue silk with pleats made laterally and ending in a silk collar from the top of which emerged a very light trimming. The sleeves were rather tight but sufficient room was allowed for the exercise of rowing.

Have you ever noticed how many blouses and fronts are being made closed at the back under a box-pleat? I was considerably struck by the fact when out the other day. For middle-aged women, who are little considered in fashion's realm, a pretty front can be made by frilling some rather wide lace in a jabot on either side from the neck and allowing the pointed ends to fall below the waist line; the front of silk muslin is made rather full and finished with a pointed belt. The collar may be draped with a frill of lace at the back or made in folds with two points edged with lace. Another thing I have noticed is that mantles and wraps are short and light for girls and young women. In mushroom cloth they are trimmed with rows of white silk ribbons frilled and set close to each, leaving about an inch or an inch and a half space betveeen the rows. The collar is treated in the same way, and the mantlet is lined with white silk or satin. For matrons, longer mantles of peau de soie have rounded fronts, and are trimmed with flounces of lace or some of those gouffered or kilted flounces of thick silk gauze which can be had by the yard ready made at all the draper's shops. The shoulders are often draped with some trimming, and hoods are also fashionable. Pale pink sunshades are fashion's latest fad; they impart a delicate glow to the complexion. Muslin and net fi.7:hus and muslin collars trimmed with lace and embroidery are still, one might say, too much worn. I would remind you that one important point to remember in connection with the cleaning of coloured embroideries is that you may restore and brighten the colours by careful washing, but colour that has been dest:oyed by using too hob an iron can never be restored by any means. The ironing process for all kinds of embroidery is much alike. The table uhould be covered with a thick, soft flannel and a very smooth sheet, to admit of the embroidery sinking in it, so as to preserve it from unsightly flattening. When there is much shrinking it is a good plan to begin by pinning the article by its edges to the ironing blanket, wrong side up always. Cover all embroidered parts with a soft handkerchief and iron quickly from the centre outward, to press the wrinkles towards the edges, where they are most easily disposed of. Wnen the article feels dry on the wrong side, if it is linen or cotten, turn it and iron the plain sur- face taking care that the iron does not touch the embroidery to mark or spoil it. Your loving JENNIE.

div.head: " WOMEN'S ulica."
div.p: " WOMEN'S ulica."

Very hot weather. such as we have experienced lately, 1 is never appreciat(d by the Q leen, and the change from ; Windsor to oJb,ree, where the greater part of the day can be spent in till op =n air, and within reach of the sea breezes, is a very welcome ono to Her M,jesty. The State Apartments as Windsor Ca.tle are now thrown opea to the public again, and wi I remain so until the Sovereign returns from her autumn sojourn on Deeside. The dismantdng of the r some, and covering of the more precioue objects, which invariably commence within half-an-hour of the Queen's departure from Windsor, is, in itself no light task. The keeping of the great inventory, in which everything in the Castle is numbered and fully described, and its position mentioned, is also besvy work. More especially has this ; been so of late years, as the thousands of Jubilee and birthday gifts h .ve all had to be entered therein before being removed to their permanent positions. Of late there have been many occasions when we could but rt fleet that the scanty garb of the Ancient Britons was not without its advantages. Toe molest muslin gowns'seemen almost more than we could bear, aad a hammock under some shady trees,with an awning to keep off Intrusive insects, the only desirable spot on earth. A considerable number of apop'etie seizeree, caused by the heat, and of sunstroke. have b: ea reported in London. A wed-knewn medical man 'han remarked that the febrile conditions induced by City life, natur- ally tend, as years go on, to increase the predisposition ts such kinds of illness, but, he adds, if people would only diet themselves pis perly in hot weather they would not suffer from the heat nearly as much as they do. All our fashionable seaside resorts are crowded, and moreover, there is hardly a village, howevPr small, on our coasts, which has not its quota of holiday-makers. In many cases thrifty housewives in those villrges, who possess the art of makng lodgers comfortable, ll be able, without the slightest extortion of any And, to earn enough money to pay their year's rent, by letting apartments for the:, rext eight wee`, s or so, Mrs. Fiera Annie S eel, who, in the place of the Duchess of Suther:and now becomes president of the Seciety of Women Journalists, has iived chiefly, &nee her husband's retirement from the Indian Civil Service at a charming country retreat. Dunlugae, near the town of Turriff in Aberdeenshire. She has a fiat in London, however, at Palace d•ste, high up towards the clouds, and as full of brie htness and colour as her Eastern tsste can make ir, and here she spends user illy par.: of the season. But her writine is done in her Scotch home. Mrs. St el des net consider that the poi Won of In- dian wonsen,ia whose lend she has epent so many years of her life, a.ni whi.h he loves above all others, is so bad as is frequently represented. She thinks it rather better than her own used to be, as women in India can hold property and the widows always get a fixed por- tion of their husband's goods. The position which Mrs. Steel takes in regard to the woman question in our own country, is in favour of equality of men and women be- fore the law, and of unicn and mutual help in all the affairs of life. M. Paderewski has known more than an average amount of sorrow, but it is hoped, by his many friends ar.d admirers that his recent marriage may prove a turn- ing point, and that many bright days may be in store for him. M. Padereeeki marries,/ nearly nineteen years ago a lovely Polish girl who, to his inexpressible grief died a year later leaving him a little son. To this child who unfortunately suffers from a spinai complaint, the distinguished pianist has devoted his life. Beene, Baroness de Rosen, who has lately become his wife, is a brilliant, handsome woman, well keown in the musical world of her own land. M. Padeeweki ',hi neither a brilliant nor a handsome

_ man. _He is intensely shy and reserved, and with his great shock of pale red hair, pale blue eyes, long pallid and almost expressionless face, he looks weird, and spectral, and sphinx-like: to a degree. His fee for twenty minutes at the piano is £5OO. Needless to say he is immensely wealthy. The harp continues to grow in favour, and soon few women will consider a drawing room complete without an instrument of this description. The most exquisite covers are now devised in which to encase it when not in use. These not only keep out dust, but preserve the strings from snapping, thrcugh change of temperature. Even with the greatest cafe, they are always liable to srap at any momerr, and one often puts away the harp with its full complement of strings, to find, upon retur- ning to it the following day, that one is missing from its place. Happily the strings which are most easily inclined to break are generally the cheapest to buy, the thicker and more expensive ones being stronger and more durable. Extra strings should be carefully pre- served in envelopes, or pieces of linen ;greased with aimord oil. Yachting gowns are in full swing at all the leading modistes, and one I specially admired the other day was of fine white s-rge, lined with scarlet silk. On the plain skirt an apron effect was gidan by some fine braid- !mg in white and gold, and there was a very smart sailor collar, lined, and hemmed with an inch wide band of scarlet silk, and fastened in front with a scarlet silk ! sailor knot tie. The tightly fitting sleeves of this gown ! were particularly pretty, being trimmed throughout ! their entire length alternately with very nareow white and gold braid, kni turned bick at the wrists with tiny cuffs of scaslet siik. To wear with this gown, a deck cape had been provided, lined with scarlet si'k. The fan is usually only an accessory the function of which is to supplement words in expressing emotions, asking questions, corroborating or denying statements, etc., etc. But the present weather has unearthed its original purpose, and at " crushes " dinner parties, theatres, and concerts, we are using our fans with view to cooling ourselves. There is no prevailing fashion in these particular weapons. Large and small,feathered and gauze, al! appear to flourish alike. When a sharp pain begins to m .ke itself felt in the busy woman's forehead, and a dull ache in the back of her neck, there is only one thing for her to do. This is —get out of any tight clothes, coil her hair losely on the top of her bead, and bathe her face and neck for five minutes in the hottest water she can bear. After that she should lie down on her back and rise at the en &of half-an-hour, when she will feel ten jean younger. Add a little salt, and water, and cook till tender, using only jest enough water to keep the cucumber frcm burning. Put a pint of milk on the fire and when it boils add two tablespoonfuls of flour that have been made into a smooth paste with some milk. When it is the consis- tency of crean add the cucumber, well drained. Sweeten slightly and serve.

div.head: YOUNG MOTHER'S STORY.
div.p: A YOUNG MOTHER'S STORY.

The central figure of this story from the " West Nottinghamshire Observer" h Mrs. Bose Bull, of 18, William-terrace, Windsor-street, Beeston, who in con- versation with a r.erorter, made the following remazk- able statement :

"After the birth of my little boy, who is now four and a half months old, I seemed to go suddenly wrong in health, and to tell the truth, I never expected to ltave the house again, except for illy last journey." "What were you suffering from then?" " Acute indigestion : I really don't know what else it cur be callei. I was utterly unable to take any kind gf food, even a cup ot b?ef-tea,withcut suffering intense pain. In addition to this, or perhaps in consequence of it. I was so weak that I could not walk acrcss the room without assistance."

" But if yow were in such a sad plight a short time ag3 I can scarcely undentand how it is you are now looking 80 well and merry." '6 Well, one evening my father looked up from the paper he was reading, and said, Here is a report of a case almost like yours, which ha a been curEd by taking Dr. Williams' pink pills for pale people. Why net give them a trial ?' My father seemed so impressed with the case that he persuaded Me to obtain a box." " And how long was it before you began to feel b.6ne- fit ?"

_ " After a couple of doses. Yes, you may smile, but it is perfectly true. On the third day I felt decidedly better, and after taking two boxes I was so much better that I was able to return to my husband." "And what did the doctors say about you ?" " 1 concealed from them that I was taking Dr. Wil- liams' Pink Pills, and I'm sare they could not make out why Iso suddenly took a turn for the better. My hus- band was both delighted and astonished to see me about again, and my neighbours could hardly believe their eyes. I have taken two more boxes, making four in all, and lam now as strong and well as ever I was in my life." Often treated as a trivial ailment, indigestion is one of the most intractable of diseases. Th e remedy to be sought is something that will enable the system to assi- milate and derive benefit from the food taken, which is the characteristic effect of Dr. Williams' pink pills. Sum- mer weather often starts indigestion; when its effects are felt, do not fly to purgatives. which at the best only give temporary relief, but use Dr. Williams' pink pills, paying careful attention to the directions. They have cured many other ailments—impoverished blood, de- bility. St. Vitus' dance, consumption, rheumatism, &c. Where there is anyOfficulty placed in the way of ob- taining the genuine pills, readers should note that the latter always bear the full rame. div.head: THY EXAMINER, FRIDA.Y, JULY 21, 1899
div.p: THY EXAMINER, FRIDA.Y, JULY 21, 1899
REVENGE OF VALERIE:
A ROMANCE OF BRITISH COLUMBIA.
BY HUME NISBET,
Author of "A Sweet Sinner," "Bail Up," "The Rebel Chief," "Rings of the Sea," 'Hunting for Gold, "The Swampers,"

Sir Lewis Eastlake, twenty-four years of age, is introduced to the reader, as he is "going the pace," i at a London gambling club. There, n company with a friend, Captain Eric St. Arnoul, he gets into an altercation' which results in a duel, at Cherbourg. His opponent is killed in this. He has a strong sentimental friendship with the Duchess of Valerie, at Genoa, a widow lady,in the prime of her beauty, who, in affection for him, backs the financier, who tends him money.

"And this doctor? Is he the best man to look after such a patient ?" "'The very best, Valerie. Besides, all that is required will be rest for a few days. There.is positively no danger for Lewis." .."Thank Heaven. Forgive me, Mc, my natural fears. You know my secret." She was once again composed, yet considerably paler than before. Her eyes also now became dewy with emotion, and so lost their fire. "Yes!" murmured Eric gently, looking at his cousin keenly. "Between your natural fears and your hound's natural anxiety to taste my calves, I feel decidedly at home in the Villa Idumea ; and would sooner have faced a menagerie than the pair of you, if I carried any serious evil tidings." . At this moment the gong sounded for dinner, and offering his arm, upon which she again placed her hand, this time with the conventional light touch, he led her towards the door, which the retainer had now opened and was waiting at. Half-way across the vast chamber she suddenly paused, and whispered in his ear: "What was the quarrel about—a woman?" "No.! Cards," he murmured softly under his moustache, with a gentle smile. She was also smiling placidly, as they passed down the wide, high staircase, between the line of powdered, bent domestics, to the dining-room. She chatted gaily the small talk of their society, while he answered like the well-bred gentleman he was. Throughout the dinner they chattered on about light and indifferent subjects, while the servants were present. Afterwards he rose when she did, and accompanied her to her cosy sitting-room, where, with coffee and cigarettes and the domestics excluded, they resumed their previous conversation. The Duchess Valerie did not treat her cousin Eric with much more consideration than poor rela- tions usually receive at the hands of those they are dependent upon. She was the patroness, and he the client. Neither was she troubled with much shyness in discussing her heart affairs with him. He placed her footstool devotedly under her feet, and lit .her cigarette, then he waited obediently for his instructions. Although so soft-skinned and youthful-looking, anyone could see that she was the ruling mind. Not alone by reason of her position and wealth, but by the passionate directness and clear force of her character. With the man she was infatuated upon, she might be yielding and weak, but not with her cousin Eric. _ _ _ .

...„......_ ____. "Now, cousin, tell me exactly bow that unfortu- nate quarrel took place; also if you were present, as I suppose you were, why did you not prevent it from going farther than words ? " Eric, the gentlemanly club-lounger and black- leg, told his story glibly. He placed all the blame on the other man, and prudently left out that it was his hand which had been originally challenged, while his hot-headed and chivalrous friend, Sir Lewis Eastlake, had drawn the dispute from him, and changed an ordinary club-room argument into an insult and a challenge. Not another intimate of Eric St. Arnoul would have interfered as Sir Lewis had done. They knew hint too well. He told her that he had tried his utmost to keep his friend out of it. But when wine is in, wit is out, and a blow in a club-room is too serious a matter, even at the end of the nineteenth century, for gentlemen to pass over with an apology. His hand was out, straight from the sboulder, and young Bingham on the carpet, before any one could interfere. "Like you, sweet cousin, Sir Lewis is apt to think afterwards." "It was unfortunate, for you, as for him." "I know," replied Eric moodily. "You needn't remind me, Valerie, about it. I'd have given a lot to have prevented that meeting across the Channel. If you knew my condition of mind, when I saw those men facing each other, between the counting of the time and the firing, you'd have pitied me. By Jove! it felt as if the bullet had gone into my own carcass, when I saw Lewis fall backwards. I did not think of the other fellow, any more than you do now, although, from all I hear, his case is pretty critical. I only saw Lewis—" "—and thought doubtless, ' there goes my chance of an annuity, ' " interrupted the Duchess Valerie, with compressed lips and sombre brown eyes. She was looking at him; no longer the gentle lady, but with jaws almost as squarely defined as his own. "Yes, I confess it, those were my thoughts," he answered, with a short, bard laugh. "The very best motive you could have for me to look after my charge. His life was the most precious thing I could think about, and I was as eager to save it, as you could be; perhaps more so—" ',No, Eric, not more so. His life is mine. I feel his wound in my neck now. Aye, in my heart as well," answered her grace, placing her hand on her left breast. "If he had been killed, I think I should have murdered you for not going between him and the fatal bullet. You know my senti- ments. Bring this man to me, for life, and I will purchase you an annuity of five thousand a year— you say that will content you, Eric, therefore bring him to me. He is poor, and I have bought him up already, but I want his love—his heart. Not alone his hand." She rose and swept out her lovely arms in a paroxysm of passion. , "I would conquer a world to win my love, my Lewis, my soul's desire. I have fixed my heart upon him, and him only. My heart, my soul, my life cry out for him. He loves me a little, I think. I know that he has friendship for me, and some admiration—all men admire me. You must bring him to me, Eric, and I will win him to myself." Captain St. Arnoul looked at his beautiful young cousin with mild wonder and a feeble pity. Her gusts of passion seemed singularly primitive to his nineteenth century apathy. Her keen instinct and worldly acumen for a bargain also troubled his languid mind, as much as it could be troubled. If she would only act consistently, he might know what to do; ,but who could manage such a bundle of untutored nerves—a woman like Juliet and Cleopatra fused together one minute, and ' a financial, hard-headed broker the next? " "Ah! " she sighed deeply as she sank down again on her easy chair; then looking up at his puckered brow, she burst out laughing. "You are a sad failure, Eric. That Norman blood in your veins is degenerate. You can neither make bargains for yourself, nor hold on to what your hungry ancestors gripped for you. It has become thin and cold also, that ancient stream which once ran red and fierce, so that the holders of it cannot rise above paltry meannesses and small, cowardly vices. Now, what would you do if I gave you a cheque for five hundred pounds ? " "Do?" retorted the Captain with sudden anima- tion. "Why go to Monte Carlo, and work my new system ; it's as safe as the bank---1" "Of Monte Carlo," interrupted Valerie, mock- ingly. - "As any bank; but it requires five hundred to work it properly." "Exactly; that was the sum your last system required to break the bank, and yet—" Captain Eric flushed and gnawed at his moustache, on which his cousin again laughed. "Never mind, cousin. I will not torment you any more for what you cannot help. Thanks to my half-Dutch mother and her Jewish father, I am able to spare you this five hundred to try your new system with. Only 1 want you to take me as far as Cherbourg and introduce the doctor who is attending to Lewis; then, if his report is favour- able, I shall run over to London and look after some business, while you go to Monte Carlo." "You are a wonderful girl, Valerie. I wish you could teach me how to make money." "No, I cannot teach you that, Eric; it is in my blood, as to spend recklessly is in yours. But I 1 hope to be able to teaoh you one thing." "What is that? " i "How to earn an annuity of five thousand I pounds."
CHAPTER IV. VALERIE GETS A SURPRISE.

The Duchess Valerie was an unconventional young lady in most of her habits, and considerably advanced in her ideas of sex emancipation. Of course, however, because she was a duchess, instead of being a duke, and young and lovely instead of being old and commonplace-looking, she had several appendages to carry with her when she travelled— to wit, !besides her other domestics, a highly- respectable silver-haired and sedate companion, whose maternal appearance satisfied society. That the young duchess paid as much heed to her sheep- dog, as if she had been a piece of needful furniture, did not matter. The patient sheep-dog was there, and that was the whole that society demanded. On the evening that Captain St. Arnoul arrived instead of Sir Lewis Eastlake, this clues= had been confined to her own apartment with a sick head- ache. To have these headaches at certain times was as much a part of her duties as to look the acme of respectability, always, in or out of the presence of her grace. The temperament of the Duchess, although ap- parently contradictory and dual, was by no means uncommon with astute and nassionate natures.

rine was not at au i impulsive, although headstrong and as persistent in her affections as she was cool, far-seeing and determined in her calculations. When she made up her mind to a step in business she was not at all frightened at temporary losses or discouragements, but backed her own judgment, and, as she had almost unlimited wealth to back herself, she was able to brave the market and win. An English aristocrat's daughter, on her father's side; on the mother's side she descended from a long line of semitic money-makers. The lineage was doubtless much more ancient and pure than that of the Anglo-Norman gentleman, who was able to restore the splendour of his decayed estate with the shekels of the Oriental. But the Dutch-Jew wife bestowed more upon her mild and courtly husband than those golden stores, when she gave him such a daughter. Full of vitality, imperious will and Eastern beauty, with the financial instincts of a Rothschild and the fervour of a savage child of Nature, she was a woman to admire in all her moods, respect a good deal, and fear just a little. To Eric, her impecunious cousin, she exhibited the tigress side sometimes, therefore he respected her, with considerable dread. He admired her possessions vastly, yet he was not at all envious of her partiality for his friend Sir Lewis; on the whole, he much rather preferred to work for that modest annuity than to try the useless game of com- peting for the entire possessions with the hand of her grace into the bargain. "She is a splendid type of womanhood, is Cowin Valerie," he thought as he watched her varied moods. "Something like what Cleopatra may have been when they unrolled her from the bale, to exhibit to Coma% She is also a regular female Midis for making money; but for all that, I hope Lewis mpy take her. I'll be satisfied with a small slice of the golden apple." The next day they departed for England, vid Cherbourg—her grace to see if the man whom she honoured by loving was as safe and comfortable as money :could make; and her cousin to make all inquiries for her and take away the awkwardness of her going there. Her dog, her companion, maid, courier and other attendants also travelled with her grace, which proved to the natives of Cherbourg that some personrge had come to visit this naval stronghold. Much as her grace would have liked to have rushed to the :bedside of the wounded ye,ung. man, this was one of the few actions she could not do by reason of her station. She had no right, as yet, to display more interest in his welfare than any ordinary a^quaintances. This was forced upon her painfttl]y, whi'e she waited in the hotel, all im- patience on the return of her cousin. At his advice she had curbed her own impulse and sent him where she would fain have flown herself. No. This friendship had not been very pro- nounced in the past. Sir Lewis had been kind, flattering, and politely attentive. But then she had been his friend's wife, and as an honourable man he could not shew any more at that time. They had corresponded, as society people do, both before and after the death of the Due. But, as she now remembered, it was not Sir Lewis who commenced the correspondence, and his letters were all replies. "Oh no matter," she muttered, biting her red lips. "Let him say afterwards, if he likes, that I courted him. He has no other entanglement Eric tells me, so that my chances are good now, and I shall watch that no one comes between us."

Her chances were good now that these many letters had made the writers familiar enough to call each other by their Christian names. Letters are rare propinquity-promoters, as well as good breach of promise evidences. If a man once yields to answer the points in a lady's letters he need not be astonished if matrimony be the result. If her watcher, Eric St. Arnoul, was right, and his deluded friend had no other love affair on hand, her chances were almost certainties. Her beauty, youth, ardour, keen wit and vast wealth held out as the baits to a young man stony-broke and in disgrace, it wanted only one other feather- weight to turn the scale in her favour. That feather-weight was given to her within the next few minutes.

...... Dr. Waldred returned with her cousin. He was a grave, pale-faced, and plain-looking man of about thirty-five, with grey eyes. He had a good pro- fessional air and manner, and looked exactly what he was—a hard worker. His house was a little way out of the town, and here he had taken :this patient partly to look after him, and partly to screen him from unpleasant inquiries. His report respecting Sir Lewis was favourable, but his adversary was mortally wounded, and although not yet dead, his hours were numbered. "We can depend upon the witnesses being as discreet as possible, your grace, but we cannot avoid inquiries now that this affair is ending fatally. Mr. Bingham's friends have been apprised of his condition, and I fear that Cherbourz will not be a safe hiding-place for Sir Lewis Eastlake." "How soon can he be removed with safety ? " asked the Duchess calmly. "In two or three days from now," replied the doctor. "He only requires nursing--he hardly requires medical help." "Have you a good, discreet nurse, Dr. Waldred ? " "Yes, my sister is looking after him, and I caa depend on her discretion more than upon that of a stranger." The Duchess Valerie looked at the unattractive, but clever face of Dr. Waldred, and had a mental portrait of his sister thrown up within her mind. She saw there a woman of the Aunt Jane type, some years older than the doctor, with faded eyes, sallow complexion, and thin, ungraceful figure. A kind, attentive, and capable nurse, and as safe as a mother might be with her patient. She was satisfied with the image that her own mind had conjured up and photographed. "Good," she said. "I have an estate at Falaise, which is very healthy, with a comfortable château. There he would be safe for a time, and he could be taken by carriage perhaps sooner than you say—if your sister could accompany him." "Yes, my sister will be pleased to do so. I shall also see that he is safe on the way by going with them. In this case he can take the journey to- morrow." .

"Then it is arranged. I have to go to London on some urgent business with my English agent, but my cousin here will act as host during my absence. I move about a great deal, therefore my houses are always prepared for me or visitors. Eric, you will attend to this, I know." Filled with her self-conjured vision of that skil- ful, but elderly and plain-faced, sister of this homely-looking doctor; full, also, with her benevo- lent projects towards the beloved invalid, who to- morrow would be under her roof, the young Duchess was in her most gracious and happy mood. She resisted the desire to see him before she left, in case that her visit to the doctor's house would attract too much attention. A duchess is not like a dairymaid. She cannot steal out to visit her lover without comment, and all Cherbourg knew already who she was, thanks to the landlord whose hotel she patronised. He was not in danger, and she was going to England entirely on his account. When that business was settled, she would return and take him in hand. She wrote out the cheque for Eric which she had promised him, and a note for the housekeeper, which she also gave her cousin to deliver. "You will wait for my return before you go to the Riviera, Eric," she observed, and her cousin replied cheerfully: "Of course." _ _

He anticipated pleasant enough times at Falaise, dull as it was. He had been there before, and knew that there was good shooting on the estate, and he knew likewise that his cousin would not be long in relieving him of his duty. A little seclusion just at present was as needful almost for him as it was for his wounded friend. There would be a wild outcry amongst the rela- tions of the dying man, and plenty of kind club friends to give them both away. Yes, Falaise would serve nicely just now, and after that he might lose himself for a time among the crowd at Monte Carlo until this storm blew over. Captain Eric St. Arnoul chuckled gently to him- self as he thought about the numerous unpaid debts that he had left behind. It was not often he had as good an excuse for forgetting to settle them. Therefore, having arranged with Dr. Waldred about the time that he would arrive with his patient, he cheerfully saw the Duchess and her retinue into the train for Calais, and departed him- self for Falaise. By a singular chain of circumstances, he had not yet seen the sister of the doctor, and not being blessed with an active imagination, he thought nothing at all about her. When he had assisted his friend from the field to the doctor's house she had been from home; and that morning when he made his second visit, the invalid was asleep. so that he had been advised not to disturb him. That night, as he sat smoking and reconsidering his new system after dinner, he felt as sure about that annuity as lie was about the present cheque. "By Jove! Eastlake is too desperately smashed

up to be able to resist the shekels or V aierie, even if her personal attractions fail to fascinate him. Thanks to my constant hints, he ought to know already how completely gone she is on him; there- fore, there is not ?much more for me to do except to let events take their natural course."

Her Grace the Duchess Valerie sped over to England filled with the same happy and confident hopes. As soon as possible she interviewed her astute City agent, Mr. Stephen Belwood, and Went closely into matte's with him. Sir Lewis Eastlake was a ruined man, and worse, for unless she came to his rescue he would also be utterly dishonoured. It was not her policy to see him reduced to this extremity; therefore, she gave instructions to th? company promoter and money-lender to pay all his debts at once, both personal and debts of honour. This took some days to accomplish, for the agent had to proceed cautiously. At last it was done, the agent satisfied with his profit, and the Duchess was ready to return to the man she loved and intended to marry, with his future fate in her hands. On her alone depended whether he was to be a homeless, penniless vaga- bond, or once more wealthy and respected amongst his kind.

She resolved to keep these transactions secret from him meanwhile. He must still be left to think himself ruined and in danger of dishonour. These motives would urge him to exertion. "Now to win his heart, if I can," she murmured passionately; "and if not that, yet at least his hand. I'll force him to love me afterwards even if I fail to do so now."

He was safe at her château at present, removed from all temptations and tidings of the outer world. She would keep him there a prisoner to love until the wedding day was fixed. She sent a telegram to announce her coming, and then followed it as fast as express train and mail packet could carry her. It was evening when she arrived at Falaise, and she could see she was expected. Her cousin met her at the station, and drove her to the château. Flushed with her journey, and superbly lovely:with hope and eager confidence, she swept through the hall and into the apartment, where they told her the invalid was waiting for her with the nurse. Her glowing dark eyes fell on him first as she srpang forward with the happy word on her lips: "Lewis." Then she started and became rigid as the nurse rose from a chair and faced her.
(To be continued.)
WE MUST STOP AT HOME.

These lines are written on a cold, blusterous day in March. The wind is twisting the trees in the garden and banging the windows and doors like a choleric old landlord in a hurry for his rent. I keep stirring up the fire every few minutes, but all the same the chills creep down my spine and up my legs as if they were getting me ready for a visit from the influenza or pneumonia, The sky is the colour of a Quaker coat, and vagatond snow squalls whirl through the air as though they were hunting for people who are out without a licence or an uls'er.

In two words, it is vile, mein weather; and if I could have my way I should pack my btg in a jiffy and be off for the tale end of Italy by to-night's tidal train, and not show up in England again before the middle of May.

But there's where it is. I can't go. I'm stuck fast here. I've got to work. As St. Paul puts it, "Necessity is laid upon me"—the necessity of earning £ s d to meet current expenses. The fellows with plenty of money in the bank are free to skip off to Nice, Mentone, or Africa, and bake themselves in the sunshine, but lam booked to stop at home, poke at the fire, and fight the weather. Ah ! graciDus me; how much easier life would slip along if we could only have our own way.

In that ease, for example, Mrs. Lambourne, of Eyn- , ham, might have lived so as to avoid the trouble which made her its victim in June, 1891. It was not the weather that lay at the bottom of it, but the thousand things which comp: se the existence of the great crowd of us—labour, worry, responsibility, and monotony, among them. If she could have got clear of these when young and kept clear of them—but what talk ? We all know bow it is.

This woman, like faithful millions besides her, plod- ded away and did her duty until she broke down. Strength failed and weakness took its plane. She waS low and languid. The least exertion brought on a pers- piration as if she had been out in the rain. Her eyeS and face went yellow, and a horrible sinking feeling weighed her down. Her tongne was thickly furred ; she had a nasty taste in the mouth and was contioually snitting up a sour froth. Eat she could not—even a few mouthfuls giving her pains in the stomach, the chest, and, in fact, half over her tody. The kidney wecretion was in a terrihle sate—almost black and voided with diffitulty. Sweats at night, too, the poor lady had. You might have wrung water out of her linen. It lopked like c)nsurnp- dun, but happily it was not. She grew so weak she held on to the furniture as she tottered across the room. And nervous ! WhY. she worried over the ticking of the clock. The doctor said it was her liver, and, in part, anyway, he wad right. But he failed to help her.
In September, 1891, she began attending the Oxford

infirmary as an out patient; and continued for si% weeks. But nothing came of it. In January, 1892, sbe had influenzl, which left her so weak that she thought she vas going to die. She had to battle for her breath, and her pulse beat as if it would bur3t the skin. Frani a big, stout woman, she had shrunk until you might have picked her up in your arms like a baby. "This was the condition I was in at Whitsuntide, 1893," she says. "Then a lady who was on a visit to our village came to see me. Taking notice (who could help it ?) of how bad I was she said she believed slis knew a medicine that would do me good—camel'', Mother Seigel's Syrup. On this she told what wonders It had done for others handled as I was. In short, sirs inspired me with hope and faith in it.

"Indeed, she did more ; she went herself to Messrc Sawyer and Sons, the grocers, and bought me a bottle. It did me good, as the lady promised. In a few days I was better; I cnuld eat .a bit, and digested it. To be brief Mother Seigel's SyruP SOOR got me out of bed, and in a short time it had rag sound and well. Thank God for this medicine and the good messenger he sent to make it kitown to me. I want to tell others about it, and that is why I write this letter and am willing to have it published."—(Signed) (Mrs.) ANN LAMBOURNE, Newland Street, Eynshault Oxford.

Is not that good reading ? In very truth it is ; reading to cheer U 3 up. We can't all have our ovin way and ran when the wild winds Wow and disease vades. But we can stop where we are and get which is even better sometimes. Try Mother Seigel° Syrup.

div.head: CHAPTER 111.
div.p: CHAPTER 111.
A DISAPPOINTMENT POE VALERIE.

"Captain St. Arnoul, " murmured the sleek domestic in a velvety voice, as he moved to one side, to permit the newly arrived visitor to enter. The Duchess looked expectant still, and smiling as she advanced with outstretched hands to greet her cousin. But a moment longer undeceived her. The man she had waited for had not come, _

A pallor, - like grey ashes, crept over her face, and stole from it its radiant glow. Her eyes lost their seductive softness and warmth, and grew hard and cold. Yet her lips continued smiling with the forced society smile that courtesy demanded. "It's so good of you to come, Eric, but where is Sir Lewis Eastlake ? "

"An accident has detained him, but he sent me on to explain. "An accident nothing serious, I trust? Antonio," this to the servant, who stood by, "tate Captain St. Arnoul to his room. You rave just time to dress before dinner, cousin, so I must wait to hear your news till afterwards. I take it that Sir Lewis will be here soon ? "
"Oh, yes; in a few days, he hopes." "Will you take tea ? "

"No, tfiank you." She was smiling upon her guest as he went out, while her dog Paris also shewed his teeth, in that unpleasant way dogs have of also staffing upon people they don't like. It was clear that Paris did not admire Captain Eric St. Arnoul, gentle- manly and well-groomed as he undoubtedly was. Society young men are all so much alike now in their habits, costume, and mode of wearing their hair, that it is difficult to pick out the true from the counterfeit from the outside apperance. Captain St. Arnoul wore the recognised traveller's suit when he first appeared, and he would be back presently, clad in the orthodox, superior waiter's livery. He was tall and splendidly built, easy in his gestures and subdued in his manners; pale- faced, and having good features, would ba con- sidered handsome, and moustachios of the same size and thickness that may .be seen on nearly every young man about Pall Mall, Piccadilly, and Regent-street shaded his upper lip, while the rest of his face was clean shaved. Being black-haired, the shaven portion of his face had a bluish shade, which added to his general pallor. The eyes also were black and rather deep set, and while the fore- head was narrow and sloping, the lower jaw looked heavy and somewhat grim in comparison ; 'other- wise he had no particular characteristic to -mark him from his fashion-stamped society friends at the first general glance. It was a mighty disappointment to the young Duchess to find this substitute instead of the visitor she had waited so confidently for all day. She was not accustomed to disappointments, therefore she felt this one all the more acutely. But still, Eric was here, who had been so lately and so often with him, therefore she could talk about this absent knight, if not with him, and that was a, least something. A kind of reflection to the plea sure that was postponed. She did not trouble greatly about the slight accident • her mind flew to the two letters, one of which she had put into the fire and the other into her bosom; she smiled as she thought it would most likely turn out to be the usual accident of a turf-loving young man—lack of money. "Belwood has been too cautious, and put him off until my answer comes. Bother these penurious money-lenders I " Nevertheless, although she was still hopeful. her maid found a difference in the lovely Duchess that evening to the gracious mistiess of the afternoon. Before tea this handmaid had been praised for her dexterity and good taste. To-night the Duchess called her stupid and clumsy, found fault with the dress which she had previously decided to wear, and by many other signs exhibited her disgust at untowai d Fate. The maid read the signs and swallow ed her own resentment discreetly, as maids do who w Lit upon mistresses possessed of nerves. "I wish Sir Lewis had come to-night!" mur- mured the maid inwardly and sadly, as she furtively watched her ; ran's discontented face. "Gentlemen ought to have some consideration for the like of us, and try to keep their promises." When the Duchess entered the reception room, she found her cousin standing with a chair between him and the snarling, lurid-eyed wolfhound. A footman also was standing holding the dog back by his massive silver collar. "Be quiet, Paris," she said, touching him on the head, then to the domestic: "Take him outside and chain him up; he does not appear to like the Captain." The Captain grinned in a ghastly fashion as he replied: fancy it's the other way about, and that he is rather too fond of my person, for pure platonic comfort." There was a slight family likeness between the Anins. Both were dark, only whereas she was fresh and vivid in her flashing lovelin( ss, he was sallow, hard-featured, and a good deal worn by his experiences of life. She appeared three or four years younger than her actual age. He ten years older than what he was, namely, twenty-seven. Innumerable minute crowsfeet wrinkles were round the deep-set, bistre-shaded eyes, a well-marked fur- row swept from each nostril rcund the moustachios, while the narrow brow had a habit of moving into wrinkles and furrows. His ears also were large and outstanding, which took away all resemblance between the pair after the first look. Notwithsanding these tell-tale evidences of a hard-spent life, Captain Eric ISt. Arnoul was a remarkable gentlemanly man of the Mephistophelian order. He had a ready smile, which revealed snow-white, even teeth. His eyes were brilliant if deep-set, and his voice soft and deep-toned. When the door closed behind Paris and his

keeper, the Duchess turned to her cousin and said curtly: "Well, Eric, and why has your friend Lewis not accompanied you?" Eric St. Arnoul looked at his wealthy cousin anxiously. She had been his banker, and he her agent for some years now, therefore it was his interest not th raise her quick temper. He replied somewhat timidly: "The fact, is, Valerie, Lewis lies at present wounded slightly at Cherbourg." The Duchess fell back a step, and appeared for an instant as if about to faint. Then with a hoarse cry she leapt upon him, and clutching him fiercely by the arm, she glared upon him with flashing eyes. She was no longer the modern and refined lady, but the natural, savage woman. "Wretch! You are deceiving me. He is dead. Quick--;tell me—tell me if this is true, oh! villain that you are!" . "Control yourself, for God's sake, Valerie. Lewis Eastlake is no more dead than I am, and with the exception of A broken collarbone, is other- wise as sound." _ _ _

"How did it happen, and why is he at Cherbourg ? " The colour was coming back to her cheeks, and her eyes, although still flashing, had lost some- what of their savage fury. "He had a dispute with a club acquaintance, the result of which was a challenge and a run over to Cherbourg, where they met and planted a bullet in each other. Lewis received his in the shoulder, fortunately, and the other man in the left breast or thereabout."

"Yes! and you saw him safe ? " "Of course, I was his second. He had an English doctor, who was an old friend of Lewis, now living at Cherbourg. He removed the bullet, re-set the bone, and, like a good fellow, took him home to his own house, where I reckon he will be for the next week or ten days, in the best of hands." "Alit" she sighed with relief, and removed her grasp, while Eric wiped his face with his hand- kerchief, as one who had got well over a nasty task. She did not ask how the man with the bullet in his chest had fared. If she thought of him at all, it was with hatred for having wounded the man she loved.

For many years the time limit allowed by the standard laws has been the subject of debate among draughts players, many of whom con,,ider the five minutes per move quite inadequate for the proper study of difficult p3sitions, while, on the other hand, it is thought too long for situations familiar to all players, where to waste so long a time could only be set down to dilatory tactics. As a remedy, a system allowing a limited number of moves pr hour has been advoaated, so that rapid play in the early part of a game would allow more time for study when the intri- cacy of the position called for it. Against this contention it is urged that sucb a system is likely to induce a player to skittle over his opening moves in order to secure the doubtful advantage of more time later on in the game ; that attention to the correct building up of a position is likely to be neglected under such a system ; and that a player after one thoughtless move might put himself into such a position that no amount of study would ex- tricate him. There is clearly something to be said on both sides of the question. The five minutes per move has been in existence for many years, while the limit yer hour is practically untried, for its limited adoption in one of the New York clubs has not furnished a sufficient test.—" Liverpool Weekly Mercury." A match which will have considerable bearing upon tha above article was commenced on Monday last at Newgate-street, London, between Mr. H. N, Pillsbury, the chess master. and Mr. L. Benson who advocates the departure from the old rule. The match is to be glecided in favour of the first player scoring 2 games, but it is not to be protracted be- yond the 20th game. The match is for a stake of £2O. Instead of adopting the ordinary method of play viz :-5 minutes per move, clocks will be used as in ches matches, the players to move at the rate of 20 or 24 moves per hour, the exact number to be mutually agreed upon. We have rec-dved from jilt. J. Gould. 24, South- street, Middlesborough, a copy of " Gould's Historic and Memorable matches from Anderson and Wyllie 1847," and have great pleasure in recommending to our readers as a marvel of cheapness, elegance, and durability. No draughts player should be without a copy of this work, as it is without doubt, one of the finest books on the game that has ever been published. The price is 2s 61., post free 2s 91; bound its cloth, gilt, red edge;; paper corers post free Is 8.
ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual general meeting in connection with the Northern Union was held at the Spread Eagle Hotel,Man- cheater, on Tuesaay evening, Mr. J. Smith, Widnes, occupying the chair. The report and balance-sheet for 1898-9 showed that the fourth season of the Uuion had beed one of steady progress, and that the credit balance had been increased from £1,525 17s Id to £3,033 6s 51. The county ctismpionship had been won by Yorkshire for the second year in succession, whilst the Northern Union Cup had for the first time been brought to Lancashire through the instrumentality of the Oldham Club. It was stated that the professional rules had added to the strength and reputatien of the Union. Owing to the fiascos caused by the meeting of the senior and junior clubs in the cup ties, a resolution was passed to abolish the qualifying rounds and limit the competi- tion to sixty-four clubs. In order to provide for the junior clubs, a cup competition will be established in each county, and such competitions will be divided into districts to avoid heavy travelling expenses. Under challenge cup rules it was moved and passed that in case of a second drawn game the next match shall be played on neutral gtound. Turning to the by-laws of the Union generally, it was agreed that if an amateur wishes to assist another club he may do so, provided he first obtains permission from the Committee of the club of which he is a member. A new by-law on the agenda, which was duly passed, was that " No a lub in membership with the Union shall be allowed to play a match in the County where the Challenge Cup tie is played o a the day of such .final tie." Last season, it may be remembered that Salford and Swinton arranged a friendly on the day of the cup tie, and hence the introduc:ioa st this new rule. Concerning Professional Law 1, sub-section c, it was altered to read :—" Every professional shall he in bona- fide employment, and shall not be allowed to play Rugby football unless following such employment in a bona- fide manner. If a man loses work through exceptional circumstances, he must not play until he has received special permissisu from the Professional Sub-Comnait!e,!. Another addition to the same sub-section was that a player must be following his employment for three days previous to playing football under circumstances as follows " Where a player who has not previously played with a Northern Union club joins a near club; and (2) in oases of injury or sickness,in which case a d tor's certificate must be forwarded to the Union secre- tary. Messrs. Leodard (Huddersfield) and Tyers (St. Helens) were appointed auditors for the fJr,h:aoming St,aBoll.

cellent talent amongst the men—can entertain the company in proper style. Once or twice a week the men contribute and engage a musician from the town and with his services and their own efforts the time is passel very enjoyably. But there is no lack of other recreation, for a capital reading room where periodicals and newspapers of all kinds, and a library of up-to-date books are at their service in addition to a billiard table. A field adjoining the barracks is also used for cricket and football, and during the 'aster season the men always have " Brook's Telegrams." Cycling, it is unnecessary to say, is very popular at the Barracks, and it is extremely likely that when the Australians come to Old Trafford, those who want to see the match will organise a cycle run there. The officers, themselves devoted to sport, encourage the men in its pursuit, Major Adams, in particular, being very well liked by "Tommy Atkins." A very interesting proceeding is the passing of recruits by the regi- mental surgeon (Dr. Adams). A building situated behind the Sergeants' Mess, is used for this purpose where the men all assemble, and are admitted to the presence of the doctor in a separate room, two or three at a time. The men when before the doctor, are in the state artists call the " altogether" and those who intend to join the line are subjected t‘l, a rigid examination. Age, height, weight, measurements, occupation, name, are all duly noted, and all iuentification marks on the body; each man being made to hop the length of the room on his toes as a final test. The sight is also very carefully tested. The Colonel, however, despite the medical examination, has the right to refuse any recruit whose looks he does not consider favourable, but this privilege is very seldom used, and would on such occasion most likely apply to a man of bad character. Under Ser- geant Stamford's guidance I also paid a visit to the hospital, where the men can have all the attend- ance and comfort necessary in case of illness. Everything appeared sweet and clean uad in good order. A special room is also fitted up for isolat- ing infectious cases. An inspection of the cook and bath houses was also made. The two regi- m, tits have their cook and bath houses quite distinct. The heal-cooks in charge have had to pass strict examinations and therefore know their business. The baths, I may state, are six feet long. My investigations and enquiries con- vinced me that a steady young fellow has a good chance of rising in the army. He is drilled and exercised until his body is in a healthy vigorous state, and he is as hard as the proverbial nails. He has comfortable sanitary quarters, good food,plenty of recreation and a career before him; and if he has not finished his education to his satisfaction he has amps opportunity at the school provided for the men in barracks. The school is most efficiently managed and those who desire can get an excellent eucation there without cost. With all these ad- vantages it is difficult to see why the Army is not more popular. It is an honourable service and one in which a man can retain his self-respect and be re- spected ; and compared with many occupations of the masses it is infinitely superior.

div.head: POLO MATCHES AT WARRINGTON BA.THS.
div.p: POLO MATCHES AT WARRINGTON BA.THS.

There was a crowded attendance at the Corpora- tion baths on Tuesday evening whea two league matches were contested. The first game was be- tween Warrington second and St. George's Liver- pool, in the second division of Liverpool and Dis- trict League. In the first half Warrington defended the deep tnd. Play opened inauspiciously for the home team, Bailey the Warrington goal keeper lett- ing in a weak shot in the first two minutes. Play ruled even for a time, and then Liverpool had slightly the better of matters. The referee allowed them a second goal, despite the fact that the scorer stated that the ball had not gone under the posts. The score was unaltered at nail time. Toe local team gave a much better exhibition in the second half, and Houghton and Lowe succeeded in scoring. The play was a trifle rough at times, but not such as to warrant the extreme measures of the referee in sending four players out of the water. The re- salt of the game was a draw, two each. important . engagement of the evening between Warrington and Wigan in the Ist dwiviTsihsteihoanintoosfbe League. The teams were as fol- lows : —Warrington : Robertson (goal), Cronehaw and Boscow (backs), W Ashton (half-back), Anders Hughes and C Ashton (forwards). Wigan: Smith (sal), Melling and Hersley (backs), Thornber (half- bYck), Hazelton, Eatcliffe and Delaney (forwards). Warrington defended the shallow end in the open- ing half, Anders was fouled twice in front of goal, and was awarded a penalty shot, from which he scored. Shortly after the Wigan left forward got away and shot a capital goal. It Ashton scored a second goal for Warrington before half-time, and on change of ends the home team was leading by two goals to one. Warrington had much the best of matters in the second half, and the visitors were never really dangerous. Goals were scored by Anders and W Ashton, and Warrington won by four goals to Wigan, 1.

The extraordinary general meeting of Pared Bank, Limitml. will be held at the Bank Premises, Winvirick- street, Warrington, on Thursday, the 27th of July, tor the purpose of declaring dividends t b 1 payable ,on the let August, and Ist November ; and conducting toe orrlina y business of the company. The Directors. in subm'aing to the shareholders tne balance sheet ot the bank at 30th June, 1899, certified by the auditors, have to report that the position and prospects of the business continue to he in every way satisfactory. Including, £64,770 18s 4d brought forward en the 31st Deeember, 1898, the net balance of profits, after providing for all bad and doubtful debts, and rebating the current bits at 5 per cent.. is £222,952 19s 11d. From this sum the directors recommend r—A. dividend at the rate of 19 per cent, per annum, free of income tax, for the quarter ended 20th June, 1899, to be payable on let August, £65,075 0 03 ; and a dividend at the same rate for the quarter ending 30:h September, to In payable on Ist • November, to the shareholders whose names shall be on the register on 120, October, £65,075 0 Od ; tha transfer to Bank Promises Account, £20,000 0 Od ; the transfer to a suspense account of the unrecovered balance of th notes stolen oa 23rd January 1899, £20,610 Os Od, total £170.760 0 0 ; leaving balance to he carried to next account, £52,192 19 11d. div.head: ORFORD BARRACKS: SOME ACCOUNT OF TOMMY ATKINS.
div.p: ORFORD BARRACKS: SOME ACCOUNT OF TOMMY ATKINS.

[BY " QUILP N.") Approaching the entrance to Orford Barracks, as one of necessity does by an abrupt turn round the end of a row of dwelling houses in Marsh-house- lane, it is impossible to appreciate the building as it deserves. The front of the Barracks is very im- posing and this would be more observable if it were in view for a quarter of a mile or more before one reached the place. As it is one seems to stumble right on to it, and the walls and buildings at the immediate entrance glower down on you without warning. At the Warrington Bg,rracks are stationed the 3rd South Lancasaire and 3rd and 4th Liverpool Militia and it serves as the Depot for the Bth and 40th Regimental Districts, the command] ng Officer being Colonel E. J. IL Spratt. Some 450 men are quartered here and since 1878, when the Barracks were erected, alterations have been made to the " married quarters" and the gymnasium. Curiosity to know something more—and I candidly acknowledge I knew but little—of the daily life going on inside its walls induced me to seek admittance. After a preliminary survey of my person through a narrow gate, and evidently con- cluding that I was harmless, the soldier on duty allowed me to enter. At my right hand was a circular building which I afterwards learned was the armoury, and further on were the officers' quarters and offices ; and ct my left was another building which included the guardroom, and gen- eral stores.

Whatever doubts t might have had as to my re- ception—for I had no invitation—were immediately dispelled after a few words of explanation,by Major Smithies, who I may say,is one of the most popular officers at the Barracks. In fact, I had, practically speaking, carte biancke to go anywhere,and was only too glad to avail myself of Major Smithies' graciously extended leave. For a moment after leaving the Major,—and only a moment—l stood still and contemplated the scene around me. At that particular moment I realized that I was the only individual who appeared to have no definite object: everyone else seemed too much wrapped up in his own sffsirs to even notice me. However, I was sufficiently conversant with matters at the Barracks to know that my best course was to seek someone to show me round if I wanted ta "see things," so I made a bee-line for the Sergeants' Mess. Here I found the person I was Cooking for. Sergeant-In- structor Stamford, to wit, deeply immersed in the morning paper. After I had allayed the Sergeant's not unnatural curiosity at my early visit—it was ten o'clock, let me say, and pressmen are proverbi- ally late risers—he told me he was just going to the Gymnasium and I might proceed there with him. I immediately assented, but here let me explain for the edification of those who do not know what is meant by the " Sergeants' Mess" It is the place where officers of the rank of Ser- geant get all their creature comforts. It they are not married, they dine there. Broadly speaking the Sergeants Mess is to the Sergeant what hisclub is to the city man. The room I had entered was of good dimensions, with a long table running down the centre. As the morning meal had iong since been cleared away the table was covered with newspapers,magazines and periodicals of every des- cription. At the far end of the room, and close by the door opening into the bar, stood a bookcase in which I noticed amongst other volumes, an ex- pensive edition of the "hundred best books," issued by the" Daily Telegraph "office. At the other end of the apartment was a piano, which showed the social side of life was not neglected, and close by a door leading into the billiard room from which I could hear the click of the billiard balls. Taking everything into consideration.:l should say the lot i of the Sergeant san extremely happy one. Those with whom I came in contact I found genial and extremely hospitable; they are fine well-set fellow's, and I reflected that considering their comfortable circumstances, many might envy their lot. As Sergeant Stamford was due at the Gymnasium at 10 o'clock, we at once wended our way there, and the size of the place astonished me. The floor is of asphalt, the walls whitewashed ; and in close weather, by means of large sized windows and doors running the length of the front, the building can be practically thrown open for purposes ot ventilation. And here in this building one soon realizes that perhaps the most important work in the Barracks goes on. The task of making the raw recruit into a capable and efficient soldier requires a specially-trained instructor ; and Sergeant- Instructors Stamford and Sweeney,who have caarge of this work, are admirably fitted for it. Both men are splendid athle es, for they are devoted to sport, and possess medals wan at all sorts of games. Fur- ther, let me tell a secret of which I am supposed to know nothing: Sergeant Sweeney will have to be reckoned with in the 9 stone boxing competi- tion on Bank Holiday—provided there is one this year. The gymnasium is well equipped with every- thing that will improve the physique of the recruit, tor the linesman, as distinct from the militia man, is compelled to come up o a certain standard. Both the Instructors took a batch of men in hand—re- cruits for the line and the militia—and were soon busy putting them through their paces whilst a larger body of men was being drilled in the open square opposite. Parallel bars, the horizontal bar, vaulting horse etc., etc. all occupy a place in the gymnasium,and 31b durnb-bella aroused for exercises. The recruit has to learn to handle a rifle, buts "clammy rifle" takes the place of the latter until he is fairly prOticient. When the recruit is somewhat advanced, Sandow's system of exercises, which has been adopted in the army, is used. The batch of men that Sergeant Stamford had in hand were afterwards taken outside the Gymnasium to an open space where jumping and vaulting exercises were gone through in addition to tests at "muscling up'• their own bodies from a horizonal bar. One can well understand that:this work of licking into shape the rawirecruits is no•-.. easy and the lustructors have always to he up to "concert pitch" for the men can 8301 i detect any sign of weakness on the part of their officers. The leaping over wooden p3sts and other exercises are a'l for toe purpose of finding out the weak points of these men,who,we may Eay,were recruits ranging from one week to five or six weeks' service. For infantry of the line the recruit must be 5 feet ait, inches in height, weight 115 lb., and must have a minimum chest measurement of 32 inches; expansion 34 inches, and ha 18 years of age. In addition his eyes must be good and he must have no decayed teeth. The latter restriction I under- stand is expected to be somewhat modified soon and the acceptance or non-acceptance of a recruit with that failing will be left to the discretion of the sargeon. Recruits for the militia must be 5 feet 2 inches, and' 17 years of age. No chest measurement is laid down,and both line and militia recruits mast do 20 hour's drill during the week. The effect of the constant training on the raw re- cruit is astonishing in some respects, but when one considers the good tood,regular exercise and recrea- tion he gets, the result is not quite 60 surprising. The exercises are so searching and find on., the minor muscles in such a remarkable way that it is not at all uncommon for a man to gain a stone in , weight and a couple of inches across the chest in , thre4 months, and cases occur where raciuits, even of 22 and 23 years of age, have put on between one and two inches in height in that time. In regard to recreation they are well off indeed, for unless be is on orderly duty, from three o'clock he can call the time his own until 9.30 at night, and if he cares can learn single-stick and boxing in the gymna- sium. Well-behaved men can, with a pass, remain out of Barraeks until 12 o'clock, and those who wish can go home on Friday afternoon until 12 o clock on Sunday night. Those who remain in Barri.cks, however, must attend Divine service on Sunday morning. The militia-man when he has finished his seven weeks' training goes home and the linesman after thr, e ninths in the devit is drafted off elsewhere. The ..'zien have most comfortable slteping quarters and good sustaining, and well varied food. In the canteen they can get•what they want at cost price. There is a room fitted up like a miniature 'theatre with a stage where vocalists—and there is some ex-

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
CRICKET.

Warrington were in a scoring mood on Saturday. For nearly the whole of the afternoon the Northern team were Rept leather-hunting on their ground at Waterloo whilst the Warrington team was running up the beauti- ful total of 234 for the loss of seven wickets. Chief among the scorers was Dr. Smith who contributed 77 runs in capital style: The wicket was ia psrfect con- dition, and as the Warrington skipper won the toss of the coin, he had no hesitation in deciding to go to the wicklts first. Dr. Smith and Thewlis were the initial b tsmen and they were opposed by S. E. Job and

At the outset Tbewlis did the major portion of the scoring, getting each bowler away to the boundary. Runs came steadily, chiefly from Henson's end, and at 31 F. G. Thompson was given a trial. The change soon proved effective, for at 33 Thewlis failed to time one from the new bowler, and retired for a well-plaped 21. E. Connor was the succeeding batsman, and a prokaged stand was now witnessed. Dr. Smith played with more confidence and hit out merrily, sending up the fifty with a fine stroke. Runs continuing to come rapidly, Henson resumed at his old end, but the batsmen con- tinued their merry career. S. E. Job resumed at 91, but the separation was effected by Henson, who got Connor caught at mid off, the outgoing batsman having made 82 in faultless style. J. Callon filled the vacancy, and atter escaping being caught in the slips scored freely. Dr, Smith speedily sent the hundred up, and then hit Job over the pavilion, completing his fifty amid cheers. The batsmen were well set, and at 127, the Rev. El. E. Elwell gave up the pads and gloves to the Northern captain. Dr. Smith despatched the second ball to the boundary. His 77 was a capital display. for although a trifle unsteady at the opening, he eventually hit with all his old brilliancy, placing Vie ball in clever fashion. Included in his score were two boundary strokes. He was at the wickets nearly two hours, and received a hearty reception on retiring.

J.W. Bibby filled the vacancy but Callon did the major portion of the scoring. At 152 the bitsmen tried for a short run, but Bibby fell the victim to an accurate shy at the wickets. G. Clarke assisted Callon to rapidly augment the score,and boundaries were rapidly obained by each batsman. The bowlin4 was changed at 191. Holt receiving Elwell, whilst Thompson replaced Fraser, whose slows were anything but destructive. The second century was hoisted, and then in quick succession both Clarke and Callon were dismissed. The first-named was caught at short slip for a faultless 23, whilst Callon ex- perienced had luck in not reaching his fifty, being three short of that coveted number when he placed one in the hands of cover point. Beyond the chance given at the commencement, Mr. Callon had given a stylish display of sound cricket, and his score included four boundary hits. With T. Knowles and W. H. Podmore together 17 runs were added, when Podmore was caught at deep point and at a quatter to six the closure was applied the Warrington s.ore standing at 234 for seven wickets,

The Northern team made a sensational start. The bowling was shared hy Dr. Smith and J. W. Bibby and after each had sent down a maiden Dr. Smith bowled W Fraser with a grand tall, whilst in the same over a fine catch at point sent back F. G. Thompson. W. K. Fercie came next. but the batsmen were ill at ease with the Warrington captain, who was bowling at a terrific rate. With a dozen on the score shot Ferule was caught in the slips, whilst with the addition of seven runs, G. Fraser was bowled. Dr. Smith continued to carry all before him, and with Bibby failing Connor was tried at 24. The separation was effected by Dr. Smith, who gat T. B. Job caught at the wicket, whilst three runs later another catch by Connor in the slips sent back Holt, six wickets being down for 28. With Henson and R. K. Fernie together a stubborn resistance was offered, and though bowling ehanges were tried frequently, it was all to no purpose, and at the close both batsmen kept their wickets intact The fielding of the Warringtouians was exceptionally smart, but the honours of the day fell t ) Dr. Smith, who was not osly top scorer but also the most successful bowler, taking six wickets for 20 rune.

Sankey Wire Mills, for the second time this season, eojoyed a match on the beautiful enclosure of the High Legb Club. On a perfect wicket, the home team com- menced their innings and scored no fewer than 142 runs for the loss of six wick-As. The Wire Mills were given a turn with the bat and responded with 85 for six wickets, the closure then being applied. For the Wire Mills, Marshall, PritchErd and Woodcock were the prin• cipal sclrers, whilst J. Evans was the most successful with the ball. The fact that the Wire Mills team is still unteareq this season spetks well for the general all- round ability of the players.

The match between the staff of the Warrington and Liverpool offices of Messrs. Peter Walker and Sons, Limited, is sorry reading from a Warrington point of view. The Liverpool men compiled 187 to which &oath contributed 130. The Warrington men were then sent in and just scored exactly three dozen, Sleath capturing six of the wickets. When next thee teams meet, the Warrington pass-word must bs " Beware of Sleatb."

The Warrington Catholics 2nd were clparly outclassed at Frodsham on Saturday. For the less of eight wickets FrDdsham 2nd scored 133. Booth and Holland hitting with great freedom. The Catholics on the other hand were all out for 38, Pye taking 5 wickets for 11. and Selby 4 for 25.

GRAND UNITED ORDER OF ODDFELLOWS, WARRINGTON DISTRICT.

The members ef the Benevolent Star Lodge, No. 449, having issued a challenge to play tbe rest of the dis- trict,it was accepted on their behalf with great alacrity by Bro. R. Savory, with the result that the watch came to a conclusion on Saturday last. The merniaers assem- bled at the Lion Hotel. Bridge-street, where a ceuple of 'buses were in readinesi to convey them to the Cat and Lion Hotel, Stretton. The route taken was through Latchford and Appleton. The weather being beautifully fine and the surrounding country being at its best added to the enj)ymenr of the atternan's outing. The green was in fairly good order, and the teams having been chosen, some very interesting names were anticipated, but no one however was prepared to see the district team so heavily beaten. Toe district team was cap- tained by Bro. R. Savory, and Lodge 449 learn by Bro. W. Smith, the result of the games being as below :

After the match had been completed, 34 of the mem- bers of the Order sat down to a very substantial dinner, which had been prepared in an excellent manner by the host and hostess. Mr. and Mrs. Ostler. Needless to say, full justice was done to the repast. On the cloth being removed, Bro. R. L. AND N- W. RAILWAY ATHLETIC FESTIVAL AT LYMM.

The thirty-fifth annual athletic festival promoted by the Liverpool employ em of the London and North-Western Railway CompLlny was held at Lymm on Saturday, in beautifully fine weather. The visitors, who numbered about four thousand, were conveyed by several special trains from Liver- pool. A moderate number also attended from War- rington and district. The arrangements were in the hands of a comprehensive committee, under the chairmanship of Mr J Loftbouse, Mr John Pringle, and Mr M H Evans hon. secretaries, and Mr H T Berney, press steward. Among these pre- sent in the enclosure were Messrs W Bingham (pre- sident),T thaw (vice-president sports),L. Sports were beld,and at the conclusion, prizes were distributed to the successful competi- tors by the uresident, Mr. William Bingham, who congratulated those present on the euccess of the sports and the beautiful weather with which they had been favoured.
