DESTRUCTIVE FIRE AT WARRINGTON.

One of the most disastrous fires which have occurred in Warrington for some time was that which broke out on Monday evening on the pre- mises of Me,srs. Barker and Sons, engineers and iron founders, of Ilsydock-street. Infor- matien of the outbreak was received at the Fire Engine Station about a quarter past eight, but owing to some difficulty in ringiog the bell the alarm was not given with that promptitude which is so necessary. However. Deputy Superintendent Turner with a number of men proceeded with the hose reel, ladders, &c, and they were followed immediately afterwards by the fire engine" Captain" and a futher complement of men. On arrival it was found that the flarass had got a strong hold of the pattern an fitting shop —a large three storied building—but efforts were made to save it, mere especially at the end nearest Haydock-street, connected with which was a small office. A number of hydrants were got to work despite the difficulty of getting a proper supply of water but it was seen that it was impossible to save the burning building. and the firemen directed their drone towards saving the adjoining work- shops and cottage property which were in close proximity. In this they were successful, the fire being confined to the building in which it origin- ated. The fire blazed fiercely and was not subdued until nearly eleven o'clock. The place was then a complete wreck. The office which adjoins the pattern shop was not materially damaged, and the whole of the books were saved. The foundry and turning shop and smithy also escaped, and the works is now going on there as usual. Most of the workmen from the pattern shop will be found employment in other parts of the works.Tbe fire was smouldering all night, and the firemen did not leave the premises until early next morning. The fire was witnessed by large numbers of spec- tators and the police had some difficulty in pie vent- ing theta from impeding the firemen in their work. The police received very valuable assistance from. , a number of soldiers from the Barracks. Ceuncil- lors Smethurst, Alfred Jolley, and linnion were presens, and they did all they could to assist the firemen in their arduous task; also helping the police to keep the crowd from venturing too near the burning building. 'the fire spread with great rapidity, and for a time the flames shot high into ' the air, and could be seen a long distance away. Some exciting scenes were witnessed. House No. 16 ,is occupied by Mr. Powell, one of the inspectors of nuisances in the service of the Corporation, and-as it was feared his premises (as well as the unused houses adjoining, which had been purchased by the proprietors ot the foundry for purposes of extension) would soon become a prey to the flames, it was decided to remove all the furniture in the oceupied premises. Five or six men and women commenced , the task, carpets, mirrors, pictures, boxes, beds, chairs, and other household furniture being pitched through the windows into the hands of the crowd waiting below to receive them. The task was very speedily accomplished, most of the goods being taken to Mr. Heaton's yard on the opposite side of toe street. A great deal of the furniture was damaged, and some of it was either lost or stolen. Fortunately, however, the fire was pre- vented spreading to the house in question, and the furniture need not have been removed. A similar scene was witnessed in Ilaydock-street,the contents of several houses being removed to a place of safety. The premises of Mr. Eccles of John-street, suffered considerable damage, most of the windows being cracked by the heat. The damage had not been assessed when a re- porter of the " Examiner" waited upon Mr. Barker, but it caemot be less than £l,OOO. Some valuable patterns, tools and machiaery have been rendered useless, and the building itself is destroyed. The origin of the fire is unknown, and at the time of the outbreak the workmen had left the premises. The following is an official account of the fise : About 8,15 on Monday night information was re- ceived at. the Warrington Fire Station that a fere had broken out on the extensive premises of Messrs Barker and Sens,engineers and iron founders, Hay- dock-street. The brigade turned out with prompi- titude, under Deputy-Superintendent Turner, with the hose reel, ladders, cuuicle fire escape, and the large steam fire engine Captain, and eighteen fire- men. On arrival they found that the pattern and. fiting shops, a three-storey building 30 yards by ' ten were burning fiereely. Hydrants were got to work in a short time in Haydock-street and John- street, and these were supplemented by , three powerful jets from the fire engine, supplied by hydrants from the large main in Winwick-street. It was at once seen that the work of the firemen was to prevent the flames spreading te the adjoining worksheps and cottage property. Their effects were successful, for the outbreak was confined to the building where it originated. After two hours' hard work the flames were subdued, but the firemen were engaged until 6.30 on Tuesday msrning in extinguishing small outbreaks which occurred from ti i.e to time. The building and stock were completely destroyed, and only the walls remained intacs. The police had considerable difficulty in keeping back the huge crowd which assembled, whilst a number of soldiers from the Barracks rendered valuable as,Astance. Toe office, which contained the books, papers, and plans of the firm, was saved. Fireman John Maunion was severely cut on the hand by falling glass, and at 10.30 firemen Thomas Taylor and J. el annion had a miraculous escape, a portion of the building on the Jilin-street side falling wit's a loud. crash. The damage, which has not yet been esti- mated. is very considerable, end is coveyed by insurance. Over 800 yards of hose piping were used during the progress of the fire.
TR ANGE DEATH OF A FARMER AT ARTINSCROFT.

The death, under peculiar circuttistances,h as been reported t 3 the County Coroner, of Mr. John Owen, of Ware-lane Farm, Nlartinscroft. lie left home at 6 a.m. on Friday, when he was last seen alive by his wire. Ou'Monday morning at 645 Joseph Stafford, a Waterman on the Woolston Canal, found the body of the deceasod lying unler s line timber in the Woolton Lock. He at once obtained assistance, ancl the body wEs taken from the water,whou L was found that life was extinct, and the deceased was conveyel home. How he came to get into the water is enihrouded in mystery,aud the affair has creAted a prof titirt Femation in the village, where the de- ceased was well known. Mr. Britzhouse held an inquiry .tesp:.‘cting ha death of the deceased on Wednesday evening and a verdict of " Found Drowned " was returned.

div.p: THE EXAM IN EU.
JULY 21st 1899.

LORD GRDITHORPE is not a Legislative Waste person with whom we often . agree, but in his remarks about the waste in legislation he has our complete 3YEapathy. A bill passes one House of Parlia- bent, and it is dropped at the end of the session. It reaches a second reading, and then it is dropped. At the end of a session the Leader of the House Sweeps away a number of bills upon which corn- raittees have been sitting, or which are based 11Pon the reports of committees, or upon which rn uc h time and labour have been expended. They Vanish utterly for the time being. Perhaps a few 4re:promised a better fate another year. .Some of theln have been demanded to remedy great abuses, as was the Money-Lending Bill; but they are Invept away that members may shoot grouse on the moors on the 12th of August, as, according to the old ballad, "Wretches hang that jurymen blaY dine." Was there ever a more wasteful aYstero in existence? Government bills, depart- rfiental bills, and private members' bills are all huddled into a common grave like the dead on a battle-field. No wonder there is political apathy, Ile wonder cynicism grows, no wonder the masses Cease to believe in the earnestness of political par- ties, the virtue of public life. What is the answer to the complaint? The stupid, antiquated, Chinese answer, that what was good enough for our forefathers is good enough for us. AParlia-

rent is something that comes into existence for Revell years, unless accidents happen; but a session Is a distinct thing also, and because each year's finance is a separate thing we have ordained that each year's legislation shall be so. Both parties %re to blame for this stupid arrangement, and there is not a pin to choose between them. The Situation is most unique. There is an increasing alemand for legislation. With the opening of every session there is a rush of bills. The chance Of getting a private member's passed is about 300 to 1, but what animation there is over it! At the Present moment, one private bill has been passed, stnd about two others may perhaps be taken up by the Government. About twenty Government and % hundred and seventy private members' bills will be sacrificed this session. Pens, ink, Paper, work and time have been wasted. Chinese, much as we laugh at their -larnens, and their decrees, and their wooden eannons and cardboard forts, could hardly do any :Worse. The vulgar herd in China do not believe In the sham guns and fortifications. They enjoy the cheat. But the common people in this coun- kY do believe in the Bills, and cherish hopes, and bake representations, and send deputations re- illlecting them. What a farce it all is! Here we are, nearing the end of July, good-humouredly Btailing as we massacre and thrust out of sight the objects upon which we expended so much thought and affection in February! Next Febru- -411 Tye shall resurrect our Bills and go through the 4arue farce. They will be crowded out, massacred 4Od buried again. And then we wonder that our Politics fail to interest people as they used to do, Ilkod that shams of all kinds do duty for realities lta our political arrangements! For the seven Years of a Parliament's normal existence all Bills P..ught to be possible to live, on three conditions. Irtret, that a resolution at the end of each session continues their life to the next ; secend, that they 'hall have been read a second time in order to eome into such a resolution; and, third, that any till which has passed through the House shall be kept alive and passed on at the beginning of next elision. Beneficent results would fellow.
TILE advocates of Protec- Protection and Fraud. .tion do not usually shelter

themselves behind any pre- of putting down a fraud, and it is a little bard upon the protesters against fraud that they lbeuld be accused of being Protectionists. Pro- toetion is the putting of a duty upon a foreign to benefit a home-produced article. There :144 be no question of colour, or sanitati,an, or 'lltitY in the matter. As between, for instance, 141. kind of corn and another such questions could 11 ,c't arise. , American wheat is as wholesome as 7ltish wheat. But when questions do arise Peeting imitation, fraud, and unsatisfactory sub- the difficulty of arguing the matter Zee'lleraically is greatly increased. It is not a fair :aliment, for eximplej to say of an advocate for ;Inventing the colourftg of margarine as butter, :I its sale as butter, or the equal or the superior 11' butter, that he is anxious to protect domestic otitter, for the simple reason that he does not :°Pose to ex2lude D tnish, Dutch, or Normandy ztter. Nor does it carry weight against anyone trub protests against the sale of separated milk 11°M abroad, coloured to resembla rich milk, that desires to protect British milk. Neither 31)°,rsou is animated by a Protective industrial Pint. Ile is thinking of the protection of the

public against fraud. It might be Protection,how- ever, if the effect of making fraud difficult were to prevent the sale of fairly good foods competing with other foods which were exclusively home- produced. Take margarine, for example. It is made in Ireland, Scotland, and England from imported materials. Nobody has proposed to prevent its manufacture here, or its importation. Hence there can be no protection in the matter Sold and bought as margarine, nobody desires to interfere with it. But when bought and sold as butter there is a fraud committed, and that fraud must be punished. How is this to be done? By analysis, inspection, and regulations, it may be said. Just so. Preventing colouring to resemble butter is a regulation of a simple character, and one that ought not to involve much trouble. It hardly seernsasufficient excuse for any fraud to say that many people are taken in by it, and use the fOod because it is cheap. If we did, the chicory and coffee regulations would be unsound. IfVliv..t we fear is that chemistry aids fraud of every des- cription, and that it will do so with increasing ingenuity and frequency if measures are not taken to protect the consumers. The local authorities and the Government have this duty imposed upon them, and when new legislation is proposed we have to consider (1) whether it is called for, (2) whether it is workable, -and (3) whether it will do more' harm than good. The matters about foods recently discussed in the House of Commons turned not upon Protection for a home against a fereign industry, but upon the protection of the consumer from fraud, from having a tiling sold to him for one thing when it is quite another thing. Fraud must be put down, whether it be practised at home or abroad, and more than that we need not argue for at the present moment. But we must strongly protest against the cry of Protection being raised against all persons who wish to put down fraud, no matter from what quarter that cry may come. If it be wrong to sell flannelette as flannel, and coffee and chicory as coffee,the persons who advooate purity are not Protectionists,th migh they do protect, not the mannfacturer, but the consumer. Protecting the consumer against fraud is one of the primary duties of the State, and it would be absurd to say that cheap foods are not to be included.

For the fourth time has the Old Country failed to defeat the Australian cricketers in this season's test matches. There is but one opportunity left, and we fear that it is only too probable that this too will result in nothing more satisfactory. The match just concluded—not finished—at Old Trafford was a great struggle from beginning to end. Darling and his men found themselves out- played on the first innings, but they more than made up for their earlier deficiency when the rules of the game compelled them to follow-on. It might be said truly that it was little advantage to England to pile up such a big score on Monday and to bowl and field with such deadliness the following day. We are of the opinion that the follow-on rule could be improved upon. For instance, if a team runs up such a total that the opposite side cannot get with the requisite 120 of it, why should not the captain of the leading side have the option with regard to his opponents following on? He has fairly earned an advantage,and he becomes robbed of it if he and his men are compelled to remain in the field and op- pose weakening-physical strength to theteam which is not entitled to have such an advantage afforded them. Had the English captain on Tuesday been empowered to dispense with the follow-on it is practically certain that he could have placed England in a winning position by going to the wickets again and obtaining in quick time an overwhelming lead. As it was, the Australians robbed the Old Country of all her advantage by being privileged to follow.on against tired bowlers and fieldsmen. We merely offer this as a suggestion. At the same time we cannot help but admire the true British pluck which enabled our visitors to pull the game out of , the fire. By dogged determination they accom- plished what at one time seemed well-nigh impos- sible, though their method of doing so was not one to be commended in the interests of cricket as a pastime and spectacle. To. Mr. M. A. Noble is the greatest credit due. By batting with unexampled steadiness and skill for a day-and-a-half, he enabled his team to not only stave off defeat but retire eventually from the contest with some advantage. Probably had the game been played out, the English supremacy would have been again asserted, but as things are, the honours must be considered even.

John Wesley was probably never so great as now. Someone—not a Methodist enthusiast— has been comparing him with Shakesoere, and, so far, there have been no protests. The more his career is examined, and the more carefully we trace the results of his -life-work as presented to us in the national history of the past century, the more supreme and dominating he seems to be. It is a pity that Carlyle never included him in his gallery of heroes. Carlyle's youth and manhood were in years when Wesley's work was silently in- fluencing and moulding national life, tholg,h the man himself had disappeared; and it is wonder- ful that such an acute and penetrating an observer did not detect something unique in the man whose fame he probably only knew by repute. Perhaps it was too early for anyone thoroughly to appre- ciate John Wesley. There is no lack of apprecia- tion now. He is not the mere founder and inspira- tion of those Wesleyan Conferences which take place year after year, but he has been claimed as a national figure, and one of the noblest and most saintly of England's seas. He renewed the spiritual life of England. He strove, like Cromwell, to make her great again in the bestlsense of that word. He was the father of social reform, and of that im- mense intellectual change which has so enriched the country this century. If we could hope that. the coming century would be enriched by the work of another such as he, the outlook would in every sense be brilliant and hopeful.

The amount obtained by the sale of pictures at the Itayal Academy this year has risen more than thirty three per cent. The total sum realised was £21,000, against £13,000. That is satisfactory as far as it goes, and indicates that travel is not being taken at the expense of art. But when you wine to dissect the figures no one can say it is satisfactory, except the artist at the top. In the second gallery, for instanc-. only five pictures were sold. In the eighth only four were disposed of. Of the sum of £290 which they made one hun- dred and fifty guineas goes for a single canvas. The amount harvested in the seventh gallery rose from £497 last year to £4,910 this, but the point always to be regretted is that while crowds have come and gone the majority of pictures have failed to find buyers. It is true that the exhibition has been mediocre, but so long as the market is so limited there is little encouragement to the artist to put his life-blood into the work. No doubt many of the pr.odrictions will be sold to dealers as time goes on, but it is a very small satisfaction that they can ultimately be got off at some price. They are the survival of the fittest, and represent in their turn only a small proportion of the works prepared for the exhibition. It is desirable in the interest of true art that good artists should be assured of more encouragement. The unworthy must always suffer,. but at present there does not seem room for merit, only for conspicuous talent

We are glad to see the tradesmen and manu- facturers of Warrington at last displayinri the enterprise and self-reliance which is expected of them. For a couple of years they have sat by and seen a Trades Exhibition conducted in Warring- ton by a stranger, who has reaped a handsome profit and then departed. The old order of things is now to be changed, and patronisers of the next exhibition will have the satisfaction of knowing

div.head: EXAMINER, FRIDAY JULY 21, 1899
div.p: THE EXAMINER, FRIDAY JULY 21, 1899

that the money they spend will remain in the town. Combination has done this—combination among our tradesmen and manufacturers, who have decided to organise an Arts and. Crafts Exhibition themselves next March It is to be on an extensive and ambi- tious scale too, and from the prospectus just issued we should imagine that it will easily eclipse anything of the sort yet held in Warrington. The space between the Parr Hall and the Gymnasium is to be built upon and utilised as a machine room for the active manufactures. This time we shall have a genuine trades and industrial exhibition, and not a mere show of goods produced in the town. The reasonable price of 6d. will be charged for admission, and visitors will Ile entertained by an excellent and varied musical programme or other entertainment every day for a month. Messrs. C. E. King, and W. H. Pigot are the secretaries, and intending e xhibitors can otain all the information they require by calling on these gentlemen at the Exhibition Offices, 75, Bridge- street.

Acton Grange narrowly escaped being the scene of a terrible railway disaster three weeks ago through some unaccountable bungling. An excur- sion train from Blackpool to Birmingham was stoppei there owing to the railway collision at Winsford, which prevented the excur- sion train from travelling via Crewe. When a start was made after a delay of an hour and a half, the engine instead of going forward proceeded backwards. The brakes proved ineffec- tive in bringing the train to a standstill, and con- tinuing its mad pace down the incline it rushed past the" trap" points and eight coaches and a guard's van were thrown off the metals and down an embankment. Fortunately the passengers escaped with nothing more serious than a shaking, which is as remarkable as the accident itself. A Board of Trade inquiry has been held into the cir- cumstances and it is to be hoped that the report of Colonel Yorke will lead to some steps being taken to prevent a like occurrence.

The female shop assistants of England, Scotland and Ireland have won a great victory, for the Bill providing them with seats has now passed the House of Lords. That they will welcome the boon there can be no doubt,for to be compelled to stand behind a counter for ten or twelve hours, and in hot weather too, is nothing short of physical torture. Why should they not have an opportunity of resting at times when they are not busy attending to customers? No- body has been able to say why, yet the Bill has been passed only with difficulty. Lord Salisbury has been strong opponent of this beneficent measure. His action has been inexplicable and his arguments (F) even more so. He has so far forgotten his dignity as to indulge in weak sar- casm at the expense of the Bill, but the House of Lords, with most unusual commonsense and pluck, ha not hesitated to mete out to the Prime Minister the snubbing he deserved. An agitation that has extended over twenty years, has now borne fruit, and a sorely-tried class of women- workers will benefit in consequence.

I There is a new and interesting development in "Services for Cyclists," and to the Rev. L. Elwyn 1 Lewis, of Fyfield, On,gar is it due. This gentle- man has announced that in connection with the service he is holding on Sunday afternoons "tea will be served in the Rectory at a quarter past , four." Intending visitors are requested to send , him a post-card to say how many he may expect. Now the rev, gentleman's generosity has been made known all over the country, and we dare not contemplate how many "p.c.'s" he w;11 receive next week. Just imagine the prospect before the eyes of they that are hungry and athirst. Nothing whatever to do but use every legitimate means of increasing the aforesaid hunger and thirst, and thus armed call on the rev. gentleman and demand all the privileges of the prodigal son. It's a " foine oidea " altogether, but how does Mr. Lewis do it? Not every Rector can afford to invite the whole army of cyclists to tea on Sunday afternoon—no not even with the aid of the Government's dole. The " how " and the "why " is not our business however,and when a man opens his heart and his home with such spontaneous generosity we are disinclined to probe deeply. Being a parson Mr. Lewis may not know that h 3 has said—if not in so many words— " Let 'em all come," but we hope they will never- theless.

div.head: A. CAT'S LIKING FOR PIGEONS AT
div.p: A. CAT'S LIKING FOR PIGEONS AT
WARRINGTON.
CLAIM FOR DA.MAGE3.

On Thursday, at the Warrington County Court, before his Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulices, George Brown, 5, Longford-street, Warringt ms claimed from John Moon, master builder, 3, Loneferi-street, 30s. damages for pigeons whish it was alleged defendant's cat had des- troyed.—Mr. Longton appeared for the plaintiff and the defendant was represented by Mr. Browne. Mr. Lengton said that defendant's cat got into plain- tiff's pigeon cote early in the merning of June 13th. and the majority of the birds now claimed for were after- wards found to be dead. Others were soriously injured and afterwards died. Defendant's cat was a well-known animal, and had previously destroyed birds. On the morning of the 13•11 defendant took the cat out of plain- tiff's cote. Plaintiff had boughtlhe birds from various eources, and one had been trained to fly from Swindon. He believed that at the time the pigeons were killed defendant made some admission, but nothing had been forthcoming for damages. Defendant's cat had pre- viously killed six of plaintiff's birds, and defendant's attention had been called to the matter. Plaintiff stated that he found defendant's cat in his pigeon-cote on the morning of the 13th inst. Six of the birds were dead and four young ones had been partially eaten. Three were injured, and they had since died. He saw defendant the same night, and he said he would meet him (plaintiff) half way. The cat had killed pigeons before. Adele Brown, plaintiff's wife, gave evidence in sup- port. Mr. Browne observed that they admitted a cat had been in the cete, but denied that it boloneed to hie client. Witness (cros.-examined) said there were 30 cats about the place, but they were only annoyed by de- fendant'e cat. George EW art Brown. Plaintiff's son, said that &ten- dent took the cat out of the yard on the morning of June 13th. He asked how many birds had ben killed and how the cat had got into the cote. Mr. Beemne for the defence, said his client did not own the cat. It belonged to hie son, to whom it had been given by his employer. Defendant had no know- ledge that it had killed any pigeons, and he submitted he was not liable. Even if his Honour held that the cat belonged to defendant, he-would utterly deny that ha had been told by plaintiff that it had previously killed pigeons. Henry Maen defendant's won, said hie emplaver (Mr. Mynekyne, butcher). gave him the cat about twelve months ago. He took it home and had fed it ever since. He did not know the cat had killed any pigeons before the 13th of June. Defendane said he took the cat out of the cote on the morning of the 13`h of June. His son was at work at the time. Plaintiff had never previously cotn- pleined of the cat killine pigeons. He had mentioned the fact that Pißeons had been killed, but could never say by what cat' He had told defendant that there were as many as 30 cats round the place at one time. He had asserted that possibly his (defendant's son's) cat plaintiff a penny for the Pigeons, which were the cem- had killed pigeons. He (defendant) had never offered monest of birds and never off the house. Mrs. Moon gave corroborative evidence. Noah Ceddick,a puddler,living in Lone-street said he formerly kept pigeons. A cat killed one, and he killed the remainder. He could not say whose cat bid 'Ritincl the bird. He knew plaint'ff's pigeons, and the majority of them were only worth 81. each. He had two Belgians, but oe the day before the pigeons were killed they were not in the cote. He did not believe they had been killed. His Honour held that defendant was responsible for what the cat had done. The evidence had been distin- gu7shed by reckless and discreditable false swearing on one side or the other. He thought plaintiff had made out his case, viz that defendant'e cat had destroyed the birds, and that it hen destroyed birds before to the knowledge of the defendant. There was very little evi- dence as to damages, but as plaintiff had in the first instance asked for £1 he would give judgment for that amount.—Mr. Leneten pointed out that after Plaintiff ached for £1 other birds died.—Hie Honour said he was aware of that, but it did not alter his decision.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
SUDDEN DEATH OF AN APPLETON FARMER.

On Saturday, Joseph Priestlier, farmer, Appleton, died suddenly while on a visit to Dutton, near Runcorn. Deceased was 70 years of age. The circumstances were reported to Mr. Coroner Worsley, but he did not deem an inquest necessary. Death was attributed to sudden failure of the heart. MUSICAL SUCCESSES. ZWe learn that Master Arthur Sinclair Hough, Church- street, Runcorn, successfully passed the intermediate examination in pianoforte playing, Trinity College, London, held at the Royal Institution, Liverpool, also Mr. William R. Hedley,organist of St. Ambrose Church, Widnes, passed the seniorexamination in organ playing, (Trinity College) held at the pro Cathedral, Liverpool. Both were pupils of Mr. William Cooke, A.R.C.0.. Run- corn.
SCHOOL TREAT AT WIDNES.

The annual field treat was held on Saturday. The scholars assembled at the school at one o'clock, and after f4)rming into procession marched to Mr. Randles' field, headed by the Widnes Subscription Band, which played lively airs en route. The weather being fine the youngsters were able to amuse themselves on the grass to their fill, and games, races, Acc., were freely indulged in. During the afternoon selections were also plaved by the band, and tea was partaken of in the field. At nine p.m. the procession re-formed and marched back to the schools, the scholars highly pleased with their day in the country. UNSATISFACTORY DEATE CERTIFICATES IN CIIESHIRE.

The rerort of the medical officer of the Cheshire County Council (Dr. Francis Vacher) states that medical officers of health find difficulty in classifying the causes of death in the Registrar's returns owing to the number of causes certified in some instances. Many examples of this might be given, but one will suffice ; a death of a child which took place in Runcorn Rural District was certified as due to measles, scarlatina, diphtheria and pneumonia. Occasionally, also, the cause of death as- signed is too vague, e.g., " tumour," "coma," " apncea." DECLINE OF PUBLIC-HOUSE PIVOPERTY.

At the Assessment Committee of the Runcorn Union on Tuesday Mr. Arthur Browns, solicitor, Warrington, appeared on behalf of Mrs. M. E. Ind, of the Royal Hotel, Runc3rn, against the asses iment of the hotel and premises.—Mr. W. Sutton, assistant overseer for Rim- corn, told the committee that the house was rated at £lOO gross.—Mr. Browne pointed out that public-ha:pea in Runcorn were not paying as they formerly used to do. He then gave the average takings of the house for a considerable p.riod, with the result that the commit- tee decided to reduce the assessment on the hotel and premises to £75 gross.

div.head: BIRD SHOW AT WIDNES.
div.p: BIRD SHOW AT WIDNES.

The fifth annual exhibition of canariea and mules in their nesting feathers, promoted by the Widnes, Run- corn, and District Bird Breeders' Association, was held on Saturday in the Conservative Club Hall, Widnes,and, considering the poor season breelers have had, it was in every respect a success. There was a large number of exhibits, and the q lalitv was remarkably good for the season. Mr. J Thornton, Liver- pool, officiated as judge, and the principal officials were —President, Mr Edon Speakman: chairman of com- mittee, Mr W Ridge; vice•chairman, Mr S Walker ; trea- surer, Mr G M Dugmore ;and secretary, Mr S Andrews.

div.head: RUNCORN-BOUND STRIatER LOST.
div.p: A RUNCORN-BOUND STRIatER LOST.

• A. telegram reached Messrs G. P. Ward, Teignmouth, on Saturday announcing the less of the schooner S.R. and H. of Teignmouth, as the result of a collision off Holyhead with the steamer Trafford. The S.R. and H. was one of a class of smart rveqsels built in the Strand shipbuilding yard by the late Mr. J. B. Mansfield for the Newfoundland trade. She WAS launched about 30 years since, but has always been well found. The schooner was sailed by Mr. J. Bryant, skipper, and a crew of five. She was loaded with clay, and left Teignmoutla on Thursday bound for Runcorn, her register tonnage being 121. She has often carried clay to Runcorn, and is well- known to skippers and merchants here. The crew were saved. The S.R. and H. was owned by Mr. Pike Ward, who is now in Iceland.

CHOIR SERMONS AT HOLY TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN . The annual choir sermons were preached on Sunday, when the pulpit was occupied morning and evening by the Rev. A. P. Reynolds,victr of Kingsley. Thera were good congregations. In the evening the rev, gentleman delivered an impressive sermon upon the subject of the feeding of the 5,000 from five small barley loaves. At the morning service the choir rendered the anthem " I will lift up mine eyes." and in the evening they sang Barnby's "'Grace of God," Mr. Gleave rendering a tenor solo. In the afternoon a children's flower service was conducted by the Rev. N. J. Poole, who also gave an address. The collections for the day were in advance of the sum realind last; year. Mr. L. C, Timmins, jun., presided at the organ. The musical portion of the ser- vice did not give general satisfaction, not even reach- ing expectations.

SUDDEN DEATH AT WESTON POINT. We regrt to record tha sudden death of Mr. William Skinner, of Liverpool, who was found dead ie7lais bed on Wednesday morning. Mr Skinner was the represen- tativo of Messrs Harrison, Roberts and Company, of Liverpool and was sunerintending the unloading of the brig" Andorihße. " which was discharging 17 hundred standards of deal for Manchester. He lodged with Mr. A. Walton, shop koapor, of Weston Point. On Mond iy last he becama unwell and was attended by Dr. Mc- Lennan, Runcorn, but nothing serious was anticipated. Mr. Skinner did not got up as usual on Weineßd morning and Mr. Walton went upstairs and found lum dead in bed.—Dr. McLennan having certified the cause of death as " colic followed by infl tmmation of the bowels," dispenses with the necessity of an inquest.

div.head: Sr. MICHAEL'S SUNDAY SCHOOL TREAT.
div.p: Sr. MICHAEL'S SUNDAY SCHOOL TREAT.

The adult members of the St. Michael's Chureh Sun- day school had their annual picnic on Saturday last. The party left Runcorn about 2 45 for Chester, where a waggonette was waiting to convey them to Hawarden. The day was beautifully fine, and the drive greatly enjoyed. Hawarden Park was entered at the Broughton end, and after taking an external glance at the beautiful modern Castle, the ruins of the Old Castle were visited and inspected. A fine view of the surrounding country was obtained from the ruins: B 'Aston Castle, Eaton Hall, Helsbv Hill, and the smoke of the Weston Works being clearly visible at the same instant the party obtained a glimpse of the venerable Mrs. Gladstone who was on the point of driving out. Having inspected the Church, Hospice, and other places of interest a retxten was made t 3 Chester, where tea was partaken of. The remainder of the evening was spent in Chester, the re- turn home being safely accomplished by 10 o'clock. MISS FIAYES, FRIDSHAM, AND THE SAILORS. The first section of the sailors' party kindly given by Miss Haves, of Fendsham, took place last Tuesday.when about 20 sailors mustered At the Institute. Station-road. Runcorn under Mr. W. Shaw who acted as " pilot " for the day. Getting aboar I a number of wagonettes, the sailors were served with their "ammunition " in the shape of an acceptable tin of tobacco each, and that they kept" firing" away all the road to Pro isham goes without saying. On arrival at Fredsham the party were met by Miss H. Hayes who extended to all a hearty welcome ; and requested them to visit the grounds and gardens, where by the way all were proviied with "buttonholes." Next Miss Hayes conducted her " crew " amongst the fruit and gave them carte blanche with the result that the " tars " soon had stowed the luxurious fruit get-at-able beneath their "tropes. decks." RP-embarking aboard the " wa.gonettee the party then steered a course which allowed them to" cast anchor " upon the top of the delightful Overton Hills. Then fol- lowed football, cricket, and other games : a capital tea to which every man did his duty. Later in the day there were sports and racing all priz,s of considerable value were carried off by the mast suncessful. Tba re- turn journey was commenced about 8 o'clock, but call- ing at Miss H. Hayes' on the waylback the sailors ac- corded her their cheery vote of thanks in the form of hearty British cheers. "Auld Lang Syne " and" God save the Queen " were then sung. Bnecarn was safely reached at 9.30 and all the sailors were loud in their praise of their hostess nf the day. Miss Hayes,gives the second narty on July 27th.
NEOLICCT OP WIPE AND CHILDREN AT RUNCORN.

At the Runcorn Police Court;, On Friday, Flenry Law- son, was brought up under warrant for not anpearing to answer a summons an the 23rd of March, 1896, charg- ing him with having, on the 15th March, neglected hia four children in such a manner as to cause injury and suffering to their health.—The magistrates presiding were Messre. F. Wiswall and W. Timmins.—From the evidence of Pollee Sergeant William Brewtter, Mrs. .Annie berth, Nelson-street; Mrs. Catherine Patin, Egerton-street ; and Mrs. Ellen Morris, Nelson-street ; it would appear that the nrisoner at that time lived with his wif, (who had since died) at Grindrod-sqnare. Run- corn, with the four children : Ellen, 10 years ; John Henry, 7 and 11 months ; Mar, 2 refire and 10 months: and Kate 10 months old respectively. The police offieer had visited the house in Grindrod-square on the 15th March, and found there was very little fire in the house though it was a bitter cold night. From what the prisoner told him there was little food in the house. and,the place, he could see was destitute of furniture. There was a bedstead and a delapidated sofa, but nothing of a substantial nature. On examining the children he found them very dirty and the'r baffles and hair were full of vermin. Prisoner said he and his wife slept in the bed, and the children Meet in the back room on an old mat- tress. There was, hnwever,no covering whatever (that the offiler could see) provided for the children. The woman witnesses had taken custody of the children of the prisoner, on the understanding that he was g3itig tO do something for them; be had not done ao.—Superin- tendent PAarson said he understood that theman was new living at Salford with another womalt. Prisoner said that was true, and that it was his intention to marry the woman. He attributed the state of the house ta the neglect of his wife, as he worked away from home and only came back for the week end. He would promise to take the children, awl do well by them if the magic- trates would permit him. The Bench decidel toeive the prisoner the opportunity asked for; and bound him over in £5 to appear when called mann ; the condition being that he. took the childrea to reside with him.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT THE CASTER KELLNER WORKS
div.p: ACCIDENT AT THE CASTER KELLNER WORKS

Mr. Reece Hughes, of Wivern's Place. Runcorn, em- ployed at the Castner Kellner Works, We;toe, was on Wednesday engaged with other men in turning over a large tank for the purpose of it being repaired, when he slipped, and a portion of the tink fell upon his lea, fracturing it. He was c3nveyed honv3 and attended by Dr. McDougall. He is now progressing favourably. RIINCORNIFREE LIBRARY MEETING.

The monthly meeting of the Free Library Committee was held at the Town Hall on Thursday evening. The librarian reported that the Institution bad Den opened for 15 days during Juo.e, durinz which period 1058 volumes had been issuel—The accounts amounting to £25 were passed for payment.—The question ot holding half-hour lectures was considered in a favourab!e strain. CAMDEN SCHOOL ANNUAL TREAT.

The members of the Camden Sunday School, to the number of about 400, with their teachers and friends, had their annual outing to Overton Hills on Wednesday. Beautiful weather prevailed and an enjoyable time was spent. A capital tla was provided on the bill. Then fol- lowed races, games and other amusements. An excep- tional treat was afforded hy a Welsh choir—(the member of which were enjoying themselves on the hillside)—sing- ing several pieces for the benefit of their English friends. Th arrangements for the treat were admirably carried out by Mr. S. Littler, secretary of the Sunday School.
PRESENTATION TO A RAILWAY EMPLOYEE.

On Friday morning last Mr. Hugh Hughes, telegraphic clerkj at the Runcorn Railway Station was the:recipient of a beautiful smoker's outfit, consisting ef a silver- mounted briar pipe, silver match-box, and a superb pouch, as a token of the esteem of his fellow employe at the Railway Station and an acknowledgement of his faithful discharge of duties during the eleven years he has been at Runcorn. Mr. Prescott, stationmaster, made the !presentation and referred in eulogistic terms to Mr. Hughes' worth, and wished him success in the new sphere which his re- moval to Northampton would bring him face to face with.—Mr. Newton (chief goods clerk) also spoke highly of Mr. Hughes' abilities and endorsed all that had been said by Mr. Prescott.—Mr. Hughes thanked his friends for their kind presents and promised he would make good use of them, and keep their token of good fellow- ship always before him.

div.head: A. RUNCORN BOY'S UNLIKELY STORY.
div.p: A. RUNCORN BOY'S UNLIKELY STORY.
BIRCHED FOR STEALING.

At the Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, before Messrs. J. Ocklestoni and F. Wiswall, William Billing- ton aged 13 years, who was remanded from Friday last, in order that an opportunity might be given him to dis- cover another boy whem he alleged had given him a purse containing £1 us. 41. the monies of Mrs. Ellen Garner, was charged with himself being the thief and having on the Bth July obtained unlawful possession of the purse and money. Ellen Garner said she was the wife of Fre lerick Garner, and resided at Bell Monte, Orarten. On Satur day the Eith inst., she came to Runcorn where she made several purchases in the Market Hall. She put her basket down in order that she might pack her purchases and put her purse on the ledge of an empty stall. She missed it immediately she bad finished her packing. She asked the stall-keeper about it, but she had seen nothing of the purse. The time of the incident would be about 4.30 on Saturday. The purse contained one soverien, one half soverign, one shilling and some coppers. She identified the purse (produced) as ben, and could tell it amongst twenty. Elizabeth Henderson, manageress of a small confec- tioner's shop in Bridge-street, gave evidence of the de- fendant coming to purchase six-nennyworth of football cards and changing a2s piece. The defendant also sent another boy to nurchaae cards for b;m and stood by the window whilst the other boy brought them out to him. Walter Oakes, 11 years old, son of Thomas Oakes, Heath-read, said he was the boy who went in to pur- chase the football cards for the defendant. Billington had a purse like the one produced, and took the money out of that. Re told witness that he had saved 3s and did not want his meLhor to know. He purchased seven pennyworth of cards altogether; two three penn'ortlas, and a penn'orth.—By Superintendent Pearson : Defendant did not say anything about another boy giving him the money nor did he describe any such boy to him.

Mary Billington, wife of Thomas Billington, and mnther of the defendant, said she resided at Wivern's Place. She was in Court on Friday last, and had since been round the town, about everywhere, looking for the boy her eon described as thelone who gave him the money and purse. They could not discover the boy anywhere. She also depoled to threatening her boy with a leather- ing if he would not tell where he had hidden the purse. He subsequently told her, and they diecovered it be- tween two of the beds in the house. She brought it to the police. At that time it contained £1 23 Superintendent Pearson : When the purse was handed to us, it contained a sovereign, a two-shilling piece, and in CODDeT. Why try and make us liars for sixpence? Witness did not reply. Thomas Spencer Bowyer, police constable,stationed at Runcorn, deposed to questioning the boy as to the source of the money which he had been spending so lavishly. The boy replied he bad it given him by another boy whom he describei as " being about his own height and wearing a cap." Notwitheanding the fact that the defendant had been liberated since Friday; and, that they had hem loelcing all over the town for the " boy deccribed," he could not he found. He had been to the Catholic schools and made enquiriss respect- ing the time stated by the defendant as to when he alleged the" missing boy" had been a sohanlfellow of his. They could find no one who cams up to the des- cription of the boy defendant said he wanted to find. The defendant witness found had been in the Catholic school trom the 50th August, 1898, to March 1899, and though they had gone through the registers of the school for that perind the boy could not identify his !I snot:low] schonlfelLaw." Subsequenly he charged the boy with the offence, and he replied that he had "not done PO." When witness received the purse from Mrs. Billington, there was a sovereign, a two- shilling piecs, and Eld in copper in it. —By the Superin- tendent : He had been with the boy all over the town and gave him every nnportunity of finding the boy he described. He was of opinion there was no such boy in the tows.

The defendant's father said his son was in the hou.e at the time of the alieged theft. They would not have kent any stolen goods. The Chairman observed that the purge wag found on the lad and he could not give a satisfactory account of how he came by it. The lad, who elected to he summarily dealt with, ner- misted in his extraordinary story, and denied the theft. The Bench considered the defendant guilty, and his story an invention to get out of the congequennoe, and ordered him to receive Six Strokes of the birch rod.

Mr. Thomas Ball, of Acton Grange, wrote drawing the attention of the Council to the road leading from Lower Walton to the Walton Arches. The Ship Canal Corn. pany had for a long time been working .a large steam crane within a few feet from the centre of the road,and had recently built a large steam pump directly opposite the crane, on the other side of the road. His men and horses had to constantly pass these obstructions, and the men were refusing to use the road as they consider it dangerous both to themselves and the horses. There had been several narrow: escapes of :accident through their horses taking fright and running away. The writer saw Mr. Swinton and told him about it, and in case of accident he should hold the Council responsible. If he had to divert his traffic he should have to claim from the Council for loss of time.
Mr. Swinton reported noon this matter and also s ab- rnittei the report ot the Walton-road Committee which was considered satisfactory.
It was decided to leave the matter in the hands of the Surveyor, and that he carry out the suggestions in the report.

Mr. Wood ward moved that the sum of £3O Hi be paid to Mr. W Digele as extra remuneration iniconnec- tion with Weston Private Street Works and Weston Sewerage. Mr. Wright seconded.

Mr. Davenpart said he could not understand why their surveyors should be allowed extra remuneration, or allowed to do extra work outside their duties. His contention was that while they were doing this extra work they could not be performing their ordinary work. He did not doubt that the sewerage at Weston bad been done satisfactorily, but while Mr. Diggle was attending to that he was away from the work he was appointed to do by the Council. It was quite time they did away withethis arrangement. The Chairman said a resolution had been passed that the surveyors do not undertake such extra work in the future.
Mr. Davenport said that was his feeling in the matter.
The r4golution wag then carried.

div.head: RUNCORN NOTES,
div.p: RUNCORN NOTES,
(BY _A CORRESPOND]NT.]

At last the public of Runcorn are to be blessed with a park and pleasure ground of no mean pro- portions. They have been asking for such a place for very many years; and during all that period— in which the voices of public men and women have been blended in appeal—Mr. William Handley has been working assiduously with the one end in view. That end has now been con- summated in the production of Mr. Wilding's scheme for the conversion of the Common into the handsome park projected. Without the slightest hesitation I give the credit to our revered towns- man Mr. W. Handley, and trust he may be well backed up, and live to see the scheme's ultimate completion.

What has been secured for Runcorn is no mean possession ; twenty-two acres of valuable adapt- able land " freehold and for ever" and the absolute control in perpetuity of 20 acres more known as the Runcorn Hill. By the way, whilst I am deal- ing with the" Hill," I will set the minds of my readers at rest with an explanation of the use of that " tripod " which is fixed upon the "beetle head." It was erected there by Sir George Nares, R.N., ot the "Challenger" (conservator for the Ad- miralty for the River Mersey), and is nothing more than the stand upon which he seta up his semaphone for signalling and instruments for mak- ing observations. The cnly thing I feel sorry about is that this" little explanation " upsets all those other "little explanations "—two of which hardly agree with each other, and which have been put forth as to its use from time to time.

Whilst the vaccination question is agitating, it may be as well to call the attention of the public to the fact that the position of the Vaccinating Officer for the district in which a child is born is one " absolute." He gives notice for the abrase- ment of the infant's arm; and should it not be carried out he it is who haa to see to it. It exemption is not claimed and obtained, there is no appeal but to the Vaccinating Officer, and the hap- less parents are thrown entirely at his feet—where they may appeal for mercy, if they like; but where very little will be meted out. The Vaccination Officers of the Runcorn Union apparently desired to courteously put the onus on the Board of Guar- dians, when they through one of their number asked" whether the Board would like to be consul- ted in such cases where it was considered legal pro- ceedings should be taken ?" That is what it looked like; but the Guardians wisely washed their hands of the responsibility.

A letter WM read at the meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians, on Tuesday, from the sister to the girl Antrobus (who has been the subject of two or three police court proceedings) and through whose representations a Local Government Board inquiry was held at the Dutton Workhouse, res pecting the treatment of the inmates of the house The contents of the letter caused considerable sur prise from its conciliatory tone and several mem- bers were of the opinion that the Local Government Board and Colonel Hamersley (chief constable) should have copies for their perusal. However, wiser advice was forthcoming and that course was refrained from Publicity throu e press in ampl and non-committal.

div.head: RUNCORN -REC-REATION GROUND.
div.p: THE RUNCORN -REC-REATION GROUND.
PUBLIC OPINION FAVOURABLE. MORE DETAILS.

Our representative had an interview on Wednes- day last with Mr. James Wilding (surveyor) and Mr. William Handley respecting the "Runcorn Recreation Ground" which it is proposed to make by the conversion of the Common, and gleaned soma interesting facts. Last week we gave the news that the committee had adopted the plans but then the scheme as adopted was not generally understood. Now, we learn, that the scheme is one that will at once commend itself to all our townspeople. Commencing at the rifle butts we will just take our readers across the proposed park and pleasure grounds. The first piece of ground (that upon which they stand)—the rifle butts will be overgrown with ferns and shrubs and upon the top, seats accessible by convenient step-ways, will be placed, for those disposed to sit and view the full extent of the park. At a later period the camera obscure; might appear there. The piece of ground from the butts to the edge of the proposed lake will be laid out as the children's playground. Then we come to the lake. and, in- deed, it is this portion of the scheme that will be most popular. It will be about two acres in extent and will afford ample room for the miniature yacth clubs to hold their sports in summer, and for safe skating in winter, as the depth proposed will he a uniform one of two feet. Crossing the park on the far side of the lake will be an improved " soft " road which will join the road that now goes in the direction of Weston. Then crossing the lake and road, we next reach the pleasure grounds, which will be planted over with shrubs, and net as flower beds as at first intimated, though those may come later. These grounds wlil be intersected by de- lightful gravel walks, fringed with shrubbery, and having seats at intervals, all leading to a circular niece of cleared ground upon which it is proposed a band stand should figure; but whether or not the spot will aford a delightful rallying point should the place be used—as it surely will—for some general rejoicing. The road that now proceeds on towards Clifton and forms the boundary—(or rather line of demarkation) between the property of Lord Cholmondeley and the Common, will be put back a considerable distance and the road made to run almost parrallel with the Clifton Highway and Moughlands-lane. This arrangement will add at least a strip of land nearly 50 feet wide and 350 yards long to the proposed recreation ground, and so greatly enhance its value. Both the roads will be made good ones. Whilst referring to the roads it. would be perhaps as well to mention that the Township of Clifton has been contributing about £99 a year for the maintenance of its road and never had a cent benefit out of it. One of the con- ditions of the Urban Council making their portion of the road good, we understand, is that the Clifton road be also well maintained, and though the Old Highway Board neglected their duty in this respect, we fuel that the Rural District Council will in time make due amends. Thus a benefit will accrue to Clifton. Along the edge of the Common, which is the boundary between Runcorn and Weston, will be a well-made cinder path and in parenthesis we might any its ultimate obj.ct is that of a cycle track. Both roads will be planted on either side with trees and delightful avenues so formed. In connection with thie feature we are informed that one gentlemen has already promised sufficient trees to plant one side of the road 350 yards long.

As mentioned the scheme is one that commends itself to the whole of Runcorn's ratepayers. Such a place has been de,dr3d for many years and Mr. W. Handley is to be congratulated upon the persistency with which he has fought for the absolute rights of the Common, and also for the control of the rights of the Hill (a matter of 23 acres). But con- gratulation will not be sufficient, if Mr. Wilding's scheme is to be perfeoted it must be backed up by a steady and unanimous public opinion. That that opinion is backing up the scheme we feel certaln fct. on all sides we hear nothing but assent and ap- proval. The cost of the whole is estimated at £4,000, a large amount of which will naturally be taken up by the making of the roads; but to say £2,000 for that purpose is not putting it correctly. We farther understand from Mr. Wilding that he is preparing a plan, which it i uzaested should be put on view in the public library for the general puhlic to more readily SC9 what they ari to get for their money.

div.head: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE the MAGISTRATES.

I FATHER'S ILLTREATMENT OF HIS CHILD. At the Warrington Borough Police Court, yesterday before Dr. Gornall (presiding), and other magistrates, William Cosgrove. 19. Friars'-green, was charged with ill-treating his daughter Mary Elizabeth on July 3rd.— Defendant pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Browne prosecuted. The girl's mother complained at the Inspteor's house and Mr. Hackett (the inspector), went to the home of defendant. Defendant was drunk on the sofa and the Inspector left him and proceeded to the child's grand- mother's house in Ship-yard where he found the child and her mother, He examined the child and found a cut on the upper lip, which was also swollen, and large bruises on both buttocks. There were also marks en the chest which had since gone away. The man who was a cutter at the indis rubber works getting 453. per week, was also in the habit of using most filthy and horrib:e language.—Mary Elizabeth Cosgrove, daughter of defendant, said she was not com- fortable at home as her father was always " laying on" her. He often caught hold of her by the hair of her head and thumped her in the mouth. On last Saturday week he caught held of her in that manner and thumped her and then:catching hold of her hair threw her on the sofa and kicked her three times. He had done it before and when she gave him no cause for it. That was her hair (produced). She dare not go back home. He had on one occasion, sharpened a knife on a stone and said he would hang her mother in the coal hole and cut ber to pieces.—Mis Winifred Coegrove, wife of defendant, corroborated. When he struck the child in the mouth witness said "you have killed her! "and defendant re- plied" Yes, and I will kill you to-night." He had once cut her throat which had bad to be stitched up.—By the defendant: She only got 2lfor 22s per week from him. —Constable Metcalfe also gave evidence.—lnapeetor Hackett said the house of defendant was fairly well furnished and clean. —Dr. Bowden gave evideece of his examination of the little girl.—The defendant denied everything except hitting the child in the mouth: It was well-known he had a tyrant of a wife.—The Chair- man said it was a terribly disgraceful thing ; he seemed to have lost all affection for his childrel. He would be fined £.3 and costs or one month's imprisonment.
TUZFTS FROM WARRINGTON WORMS.-ANOTHER PRISONER.

At the Borough Police Court on Saturday morning, before Messrs. T. Rrchall (in the chair) and R. T. Fair- Linaker was charged with stealing from the yard of Mr. Thomas Pilkin,ton, 3, Bewsey-road, on Eaturday, July 8th,64 pounds of sheet lead, the property of the Vi hitecross Company, and also with haviog stolen two cartloads of cinders on the 12th and 13:h inst., value 25., the property of Messrs. Lowe and Fisher.— Prisoner pleaded guilty to both charges.—The Chief Constable said that on Monday,July 10th, a man named Jones was brought up on a charge of stealing a quantity of lead, the property of the Wiaitecress Ginapany. Limited, and was sentenced to one month's imprison- ment. tie told the magistrat:s that a man named Linaker had given him the bag to take to a marine stores. He described the prisoner,who was subsequently arrested by Superintendent Monaghan. It appearei that on Saturday, the Bth July, Mr. Pilkington was in his bedroom, when he noticed the man Linaker go down into his yard, pick up the bag and carry it out. Jones was keeping watch at the yard door, and prisoner gave him the bag to carry aril then made his escape. Jones was afterwards arrested in Dallam-lane. With regard to the second case the Chief Constable state I that the prisoner was in the employ of Messrs. Lowe and Fisher, contractors. Bewsey-road, who had succeeded to the carting business of Mr. Pilkington, and was engaged in taking cartloads of cinders to a building site in Wilders- pool road. A shilling rer load was paid for the cinders. Mr. Lowe became suspicions as to whether prisoner took them all to the site. He consequently hal defendant watched, and he was seen to turn down the Old road to a piece of land in Kent- street, owned by a Mr. Wright. and to tip the cart there. Mr. Wright gave him 61 per load for tipping the cinders. Mr. Lowe, who had followed him, sent him with his horse to the stables, and told him his services were no longer required.—Mr. Wright said there was a piece of land in the rear of Kent-street, which was being prepared for building, and had been used for a public tip. Prisoner went there on Tuesday afternoon, the 11th July, with some cinders, and he (witness) told him he did not want any. Prisoner said he did not want to take them away, so he was allowed to tip them, and witness gave him 6d. per load.—Mr. Fairclough : A better plan in future would be to obtain a reciept for the money.—Witness said be had had a cast like this before and that made him careful to obtain receipts, but on this occasion he did not think of it.—The Chief Con- stable remarked that prisoner had acknowledged that he tried to put all the blame on Jones. Be had a very bad record for burglary and theft.—Prisoner was committed to gaol for a month in each case.

SAVAGE ASSAULT ON WARRINGTON POLICEMEN. At the Borough Police Court on Monday morning, be- fore Mr. F. Monks (in the chair), Alderman Blackhurst, Mr. Birch%ll, and Councillor Smethurst, James McElroy, 1, Bolton's-yard, was charged with having been drunk and disorderly at 9.55 on Saturday night in Ryiands- street, also with Ii tying at the same time and place assaulted P.C.'s Carter and Smith while in the execution of their duty, and further with having assaulted Arthur Wilson. cab proprietor, who went to the assistance of the police. Prisoner pleaded ignorance of the offences. —P.C. Carter said he was on duty a': the Royal Court Theatre, and his attention was called to the prisoner who was using obscene language. Several ladies wen sitting by him. Witness told prisoner he woule jro. z.irn if he did not behave himself. Prisoner immediately kicked him, and he proc,eded to eject him. At the door the man became very violent, and P.C. Smith came to witness's assistance. Prisoner behave .1 like a madman, assaulting both of them. He kicked Smith in the atomach wn, f-1! to the floor and had afterwards to he medically attended. Mr. Wilson rendered them assistance. At Market-gate two other constables assisted them to take him to the Police Station.—The Chief Constable : I believe Smith became unconscious after being k eked ? Wituess : Yes. Prisoner was wearing heavy arnmuni- tion boots.—The Chairman : It is a wonder he is not standing there on a charge of maaslaughter.- -P.C. Smith said he was coming out of the theatre about five to ten when several people informed him that P.C. Carter was being violently assaulted. He went forward to assist Carter. Prisoner was kicking him, and be afterwards violently asssulted them both. He kicked witness in the stomach and about the legs. He had since been off duty, and was not yet in a coniition to resume. He fainted at th'e. Police Station, and subse- quently had to go to a doctor.—Arthur Wilson, cab pro-

prietor, said he went to the assistance of the constables. Tne evidence they had given was quite correct. Prisoner kicked him (witness) about the lOgs. At the end of Rylands-street he again kicked witaess, saying "You b-- I have finished you." Prisoner was mad drunk, and it took five of them to take him to the Police Station.—The Chairman : If he made the remark you say, he must have known what he was doing.—The Cnief C instable : He was sensible enough to be vicious. —Arthur Beardsall, checker at the Theatre, stated that he called the attention of the constable to the prisoner, who was using very bad languag,e: People were com- plaining about it. Prismer was ejected.—Prisoner sad he was quite ignorant as to wha-. had happened. UNHAPPY MARRIED LIFE AT WARRINGTON.

Martin Dooley, a labourer, was charged at the War- rington Borough Police Court on Monday morning with having used threats towards his wife, in consequence of which she was afraid he would do her some b in- jury.—Complainanc stated that she met her husband in Buttermarket-street, and he thre iteriel to tear hr up. She had not been living with him since the last time he had been before the Court but he came thr atening her wherever she went co live. They had been married seven years. In consequence of his conduct she was afraid of her life, and had had to give up her work. Her husband skulked from town to town, and never worked for less than 6J. an hour. Everytime he came back he inquired where she lived and came annoying her. She ha,d not lived with him for seven months.—Mr. Birchall: Where you not granted a separation order.;—Complain- ant : No, sir. That's what I want.— A. neighbour of complainant's gave corroborative evidence regard- ing the threats used by defendant.— Defen- dant said his wife had only brought this charge against him to get a separation order.—P.C. Turner said he was in Buttermarket-street on February 24, when complainant made a complaint to him regard- ing her husband. While they were speaking defendant came up and told his wife that if sloe went to the Police Station he would take it out of her. Witness advised the woman to apply for a summons.—Defendant: this is a made up thing between them. He proceeded to accuse his wife of improper conduct,and the Chief Con- stable said he ought t) be ashamed of himself to make such an unsupported chargr.—Complainant, who was sitting at the back of the Court, burst into tears and said that if tir_ magistrates did not do something with defendant she would drown herself.—The C&ef Con- stable said that defendant had been before the court eight times. When he last left the town he went to Salford and had been br )ught up there for theft. The complainant was a hardworking and industrious woman. —Defendant said there had teen nathing else but trouble since he had been married. He hal never been in a court before he was married.— [he magistrates bound him over to keep the peace for six months, ordering him to find sureties and pay the costs of the case, or go to gaol for a month.

div.head: FRAUD ON THE RAILWAY BY A lATCHFORD MAN.
div.p: FRAUD ON THE RAILWAY BY A lATCHFORD MAN.

At the Altrisicham Petty Sessions on Monday. before Messrs R H Joynson (in the chair), and other magis- trates, James Hollins, of New-road, Latchford. was charged with travelling on the London and North- Western Railway with intent to avoid payment of fare. Mr. Thomas Atkins, detective inspector, of Lime-street Station, Liverpool, prosecutad.—Andrew Parker, porter, said defendant left a train arriving from Manchester at Arpley at 11.30 on June 10th.--8e said he had no ticket but had come from Thelwall, and he aclordinglsr pail the fare as betwoen that pace and Arpler.—Edward Kenwright, porter at L ttchf )rd, and Detective Howells said defendant subsequent to passing out at Arpley station admitted to them that he had in reality come from Broldheith. Be had, he told them, been having "a bit of a go " at Altrincharn the same aft lrnoon, and he also said his wages were 183 weskly.—The Bench imposed a fine of 301 including costs, which was paid by the mother of defendant, who was in court.

A PUBLIC-HOUSE BESIEGED AT RIXTON.—Bight men. Eli Yates, William Gregory, David Grundy. Robert Smith. Henry Arrowamith, Samuel Fowles. Thom ss Rigby, and Robert Beevere, were charged witn being disorderly on the premises of the "Old Slick Swan," Rixton on July 9h and refusing to quit when requested.—They pleaded not guilty.— Mr W J Forshaw appeared for the license, Mr. M'Kiernan, and stated that on the Sunday evening ia qiestion the de- fendant called at the "Old Black Swan," between eight and nine o'clock and asked for drinks. They were served by Miss M'Kiernan who noticed that Fowles had a deg with hica.wisich she reeNniatd as her father's. She called on him to give it up but he refused unless she gave him 21 and a gallon of beer. She refused to give him anything and the de- fendants became very abusive and broke about 33 tumblers. They surrounded the place and began to stone everybody who came out. They refused to quit the premises when requested. —Delia lifliternan, daughter of the licensee, cJrrobor- ated. She said her slater saw Fowles take the dog from the stable.—Mrs. M'Klernan, wife of the licensee, also gave evidence. When she ordered them to leave the place, they broke a lot of glasses worth 3id each. A window was broken in the tap-room. When P.C. Clarke name, the men had surrounded the place and he too'c their names.— John Metlu4h, employed at the " Old Black Swan" stated that be saw the men break the glasses. When he closed the doors, they' threw stones at that.—P.O. Clarke said the men {dropped the (tones when they saw him. Fowles said he had caused the bother, but he had given the dog uo. All the men were throwing when he csme up, and he took their names.—All the defendants, with the exception of Beavers, were fined 5s and emits. Beavers, the driver of the vehicle defendants had arrived in, was discharged. Mr. Forshaw was allowed an advocate's fee. However, if that is not the case, the procedure, as at present, of handing in the Sc long before the evidence can be taken. seems to be a very general one. DOG &T LAB,G 8.--C !miss Casey. assistant at Bradley's Cot ing Department, Random. was earnmoned for allowing his dog to be at large on the 12th inst.—Police Constable Breeze said he saw the dog at large On the 10th inst., when de•endant's wife was coming down High-street with it. He told her that the animal would have to be proyidel with a muzzle or en engraved collar. On the 12th he again observed the animal at large in Shaw-street ; he called defendauz's wife's attention to it.—Defendant explained that they had only lately come from Crewe, and were in lodgings. The landlady had left the door open, and the do; lead gone out. He contended that it took time to provide a properly en- graved collar,and that no offence la ad been intentionally com- mitted —The Chairman observed that the offence was allow- ing the dog to be at large ;it did not matter who lett the doer open; the dog got out, and defendant would be fined 5s —The money was pad. A.-SLEEPr Datvga.—Walter Hammer, of W .r:ington, was summoned for being asleep whilst in se large of a couple of horses and a Brewer's dray, at Halton, on the llth inst.—He pleede t guilty.—Police-Constable Thomas Edwards (Run- corn) deposed to seeing the dray apdroach along the road He went up to it and found the diver very mirth asleep; so much so, that he had considerable difficulty in waking him. —The defendant was fined 5s and 9s 6d costs. TPAMPS SENT TO KNIIIIFORD.— William Tho nos and Samuel Bunion (tramps) were charged in custody with begging on the previous evening.—Poliae Constable Bowyer said he watched the men for some time and dimovered they were begging. They also solicited alms from himself, he being in plain clothes at the time. B sth men were under the influence of drink and used very vile language. Upon searching thorn llfd and 71d were found on them respectively.—Thomas. who acted as spokesman, said they were begging but denied •;laat they used any offensive language. He woutd also admit they had some drink which other people had given them.— Bunion, asked by the Bench whether he could work, said although he only hat one arm he had worked in toe neigh- bourhood of Acton Grange when the canal was being cut.and had atone time also hawked salt. He was now, however, forced to beg, at he could not get any work. —Thomas said both had their wives in oourt. and if the bench would take a lenient view of their offence they would leave the town at once.—The Superintendent said that the men were not known in the neighbourhood, but during the time thy were in the cells they had boon well kept by their wives.—The Bench committed the men to Knntsford for 7 days.—Betore leaving the dock. Thomas asked that the few copoers found iia their possession be given to their wives. The po ice haying no oojection the appdcation Was granted. JUGGING num Coon To DOOR.—Charlee Ross, another tramp. WAS charged in custody with the above offence, com- mitted the previous evening-- He pleaded guilty and offered no defence.—Pollce-Constable Wilding, who proved the case. staid he saw the ma going from door to door in Handley- street, and went up to him and asked him what he was doi g. Prisoner said he was begging. He then took him to the Police Station and charged him. Eight pence WAI found on him In copp, r.—Committed for 14 days with hard labour. " NOBBY " RIB A FuhTßEtt STRETCEI IN LlMBn.—Efenry Cook, who is a noted character in Bunco, n, was again brought be ore the Bench, the charge against him being "drunk and disorderly, in High street. on Sunday,—Cook, replk tag to the charge, sad he was "guilty of being intox;cated. but had not been disorderly."—lfenry Wilson (police constable. disagreed with Cook on this point, and gave evidence to prove that whilst on duty in Devonshire-square he heard Cook swearing. Oa going to Cook woo was in High-street, he found that he was also drunk. Instead of keeping a silent tongue Ca etc indelged in further use of the forbidden language," and amongst other people th s Constable came in for a share of it. Cook complained also that some young men had been calling hina by the nick-name of " square head."—Coo a said that some young men were annoying him by calling him square head," and he turned tett ad to reprimand them.—He was, however, very polite to the officer.—Commltted for one montL'a hard labour. APPRENENDED.—Luke K cDonald, of huneorn, was brought up on warradt charged with refusing to answer a summons charging him with using obscene language on the 14th of May last.—Prisoner now pleaded guilty to the charge and said he did not appear in answer to the summons be- cause he was not then in gout work and had no money.—The offence having been proved by police Consta le Wilding prisoner was fined 55., and 14s. costs, or 14 days.—Prisoner raid he lived with his wife in Hinson's court, and ask,. I for time to pay.—The police objected to liberatiog him utitil the money was paid as he had made off once.
