div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL IMSTRICr COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL IMSTRICr COUNCIL.

A meeting of this Council was held in the Bewsey Chambers on Wednesday afternoon. Mr• Ball presided, and there were present : Messrs. J. W, Knowles. William Houghton, A Brooks, R Forshaw, H Thornton,J Johnson, J Dignum, T HaltGn, with Mr J C Sutton (clerk), Mr S Sutton (assistant clerk), Mr Thompson (surveyor), Dr Sephton (medical otlicer),and Mr Kerfoot (nuisance inspector.)
THE PROPOSED SEPARATION OF ORFORD AND WINWICK.

The CLERK reported that he had rec!ived a communi- cttion from the Deputy Clerk of the Lancashire County Council stating that the Council declined to hold an inquiry re separation of Orford from Winwick.

la reply to Mr. Thornton, the CLERK said that the County Cluncil had been in communication with the Winwick and Orford authorities and they saw no grounds for an inquiry. Mr. THORNTON : They had the whole matter before them?
The CLERK : Y6B. DELEGATES TO THE ANXIIAL CONFERENCE __. -

The CHAIRM&N moved that Messrs. J. W. Knowles and William Houghton b 3 the delegates of the Council to the Congress of the Royal Institute of Public Hsalth to be held at Blackpool on September 21 and following days ; and also the Autumnal Congress and Exhibition in connection with the Sanitary Institute to be held in Southampton on August 29t's.
ZIEDIC&L orncrtß's REPORT.

The MEDICAL OFFICE a reported that during the past month there had been 17 births and six deaths. The death rate from all causes was equal to 7 per thousand against 12, the average of the last three months, and 4•6 in the corresponding month of last year. The death rate from the seven principal zymotic diseases was equal to nil per thousand against the average of the last three months, and nil in the corresponding month of last year.

div.head: INSPECT° a's REPORT.
div.p: INSPECT° a's REPORT.

Mr. KERFOOT reported that during the past month a ssoond sample of water had been submitted for analysis from the Union Workhouse, Warrington, and the analyst report; thefeon as follows :—" TOis water contains sus- pended matter in the shape of oxide of iron, which should be filtered off. This water is rather hard, in other re- spects it is good and may be employed for domestic use." The Medical Officer of Health reported to him a case of typhoid fever at the dwelling-house adjoining the Catholic School, Btfartinscroft. The patient is a nurse, and has been in a situation at Widues. The premises are not in a good sanitary conditioo, the privies being within nine feet of the school and dwelling-houses. The
ashpits are wet, and offensiv., and should be removed or converted to the pail system.—lt was decided that notice Ixt served for improved sanitary arrangements.
SURVEYOR'S REPORT.

Mr. THOMPSON in his report on the work of the past moath stated that the dangerous place in Hillock-lane, Woolston, complained of by the Wool3ton Parish Coun- cil had been levelled up and made good and safe. A short length of road in Weir-lane had been lifted and cinderei. In Green-lane, Poulton, a further leugth of drain had been taken up and re-laid and a length of road had been widened out and btllasted with cinders.

Mr. THORNTON complained that the Council had had no say with regard to the improvements in Green-lane, Poulton. Toe Surveyor was doing the work on his own initiatlue. Tho sewer being laid was not wide enough to meet the wants of the township for the future. Mr. Havrow complained of the present system of p ty- ing the madmen and checking their time. He intended to move at the next meeting that the men be paid weekly on any thy suitable to the Council, and that timesheets be made out and submitted to each member of the district for perusal pnvious te payment. The report was adopted, and the following recommen- dations were also anproved :—That a new drain be laid in Phipns-lane, Buttonwood, to prevent the road horn constantly flooding in wet westher ; that ilood-lane, Great Sinky, be widened Ri per plan, and that Mr. J. B. Selby's terms re land bi accapted ; that the kerbs by the Green Pit, Park,ide-road, Win wick, be taken up and re-set, and the roadway drained. That the pebble pave- ment on the footpath be taken up and red cinders sub stituted ; that the condition of Mr. William Booth re land required for widening Long Barn-lane, Woolsten, as per plan be acclpted.

div.head: COMPLAINT FROM PENIERTII.
div.p: A COMPLAINT FROM PENIERTII.

Mr. DIGNUM /Mid he had been i-astructed by the Penketh earish Council to call attentiJn to the danger which existed of carts running on to the footpath at the corner of heath-road and Cemetery-road Penketh. It wee suggested that some curbs should be placed there. The SURVEYOR said it was a dangArols corner and it would be advisable CO put a few rounded curb stones there.
It was decided that the Surveyor shiuld prneed with the work.

NEW FOOTBRIDGE OVER SANKET BROOK. The CLERK reported that the agent to the London and North-Western Railway Conspany,had been written to re- specting a new foot bridge over Sankey Brook, as per recommendation in last month's report. The Company replied that they were under no liability to rebuild the public footpath bridge which had collapsed, and unless the Council were prepared t 3 at once rebuild it, they must withdraw the permission they gave for the public to temporally use the private bridge of the Campany near to that which had collapsed. They desired to be favoured with an immediate decision and could not allow the public to cross their land and private bridge where there was no right of public footpath. The Straveroa said the tender for the bridge was £45. The Council would do the other work in connection with it.
Mr FORSEILW m wed that the C =nil proceed with the work, and that the tender b accepted. This was agreed
Mr HALTON objected to men being drafted from their districts to do work required in this case. It would be better to get a contract for the completion of the whole of the work.
The CLEas said the opinion seemed to prevail amongst some members that sufficient work was not done by the roadmen.
ThQ. SURVEYOR said the late Mr.Balharry told him that he never saw men work better that the Council's road- men.
Mr. KNOWLES said they were a very rod elasa of men. THE DIVISION OF ASSETS AND LIABILITIES.

The CLERK submitted a balance sheet of the assets and liabilities of the late Highway Board for the pur- plse of dividing the assts between Warrington and Leigla Rural Diatrict Cnuncils as per their rateable values. The assets are £1,005 3a 74 and the liabilities £435 31 id leaving a balance of £570 Os 61. He had had an inter- view with the Clerk of the Leigh Rural District Council, and he agreed with the suggestion that each Council should take over its own liabilities, and then each take its proportionate share of the total assets. The amount to bc paid to the Leigh Council by the Warrington Coun- cil is £B9 5s 3i. The Warrington Council taking roller, breaker, and all materials, tools, plant, instruments and furniture within their own district ; the Leigh Cauncil to take everything in their district with the exception of the large heap of boulders lying next the fence on Mr. John Bridge's field, Holcroit-lane, Culcheth, which belongs to the Warrington Council. The matter was left in the hands of the Clerk. This was all the business.

div.head: FILESMITHS' STRIKE AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: THE FILESMITHS' STRIKE AT WARRINGTON.

The strike in the file trade at Warrington still continues, and at present there seems little pros- pect of a settlement. The " harJeners " at Messrs. Stubs's works have joined the strikers, as have also a number of filecutters at Rain- hill. The total number of men now on strike exceeds 200. An attempt has been made by one of the firms affected to arrive at a settlement of the dispute, but the terms offered were not satisfactory to the men. At a meeting of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council held last week it was decided to support the men, and , the following appeal has been issued locally : "*Filesmiths Association Strike Fund. We the filesmiths of Warrington earnestly appeal to the public for support to enable us to continue our struggle with the masters who refuse to accede in any way to our demands for a slight increase in wages which are practically the same as they were 50 years ago. The public will see that we have cause for complaint when we state the fact that after having served seven years' apprenticeship to 1 the trade our wages on the whole do not reach .C 1 per week, many of the men having to work very late hours at night to enable them to live at all. Hoping that we shall receive your generous sup- port. We remain on behalf of the members, 3 oura truly, J. Dagnall, president; James Battersby secre- tary." An appeal is also being prepared with the object of submitting it to the various trades unions in the country. Representatives of Messrs. Thewlis and Griffiths, Limited, told a reporter of the " Examiner" that the statement that the men's wages have not reached .C 1 per week is absolutely untrue 80 far as their men are concerned. They assert that they are able to prove by their wage list that every filecutter in their employ has received considerably more than £1 when he has worked a full week. The firm feel certain that such a statement could not have emanated from their Men,

div.head: SABBATARIANISH AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: SABBATARIANISH AT WARRINGTON.

"The Umpire" says:—' Doe great and glorious movement proceedq merrily apace, and Warrrington has succumbed to the infection By which we do not allude to miserable longings for the Supnression of the Sweater, or rapid demands for Old Age Pensions, or other such worldly achemes of personal aggrandisement. We refer to the holy crusade which has for its ultimate aim the Protection of the Populace Against Itserf—otherwiseithe enforcement of the noble if unscriptisral theory that Man was made for the Sabbath.and not the Sabbath for Man. It will in future be an offence, to be purged by fine or imprisonment, to defile the ethereal atmosphere of Warrington by crying of newspapers on Sundays—a munic,pal decree which, as our readers have reason to know, has long passed the probationary stage in these realms. But, after all, the unscrii,tural SOlOl3B of Wire- opolis are no mere copyists. Certainly a recent ukase prohibiting the Sunday sale of milk at a Welsh water- jug-place may have influenced their legislative efforts; but whereas Llandudno must go milkless on Sunday,the denizens of Warrington are to be graciously permitted to interview the milkman till ten a.m. And yet there are moralists—wicked, wordly people all of them—who con- sider the Sanctimonious Humbug destitute of the bowels of compassion. All we can say is, that we hope such a display of clemency—for might not the S.H. have just as easily totally suppressed the milk-dispenser in the golden interests of friend Bun. ?—We hope, we repeat, that sucia:mercifulnesq will cause the worldly persons aforesaid to be duly impressed with the wonderful self- restraint at the command of the S. H. and his co-hum- bugs. It may be that by the time the Warrington milkman is legally compelled to leave off his piercing shrieks, he has successfully roused the dead—sleepy ; but that is purely a detail. Speaking personally, we would that, instead of finishing up at ten a.m., it were decreed that the Milk Fiend must not begin his fell work till that hour—and that seven days in the week.'

div.head: ACCIDENT AT BEWSEY FORGE
div.p: ACCIDENT AT BEWSEY FORGE

An unfortunate accident occurred in the Bewsey department of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles' Works on Saturday evening, when a workman named Samuel Mansell was burnt about the face, neck and arms. by what is technically known as the" back- flash." The air coming in contact with the flame forced it outwards, for the moment enveloping the unfortunate workman. He was conveyed to the Infirmary, and detained, but is now progressing favourably. BANK QUAY MODEL YACHT CLUB. The third regatta in connection with the above club took place on Saturday in the Sankey Canal, at Sankey Bridges. The yachts were sailed in three classes, two feet, three feet, and the big class, in which the four and five feet yachts sailed together, The handicap was two feet to the inch length measurement in every hundr ad yards, and the course sailed was four hundred yards. in the two feet class, there were six entries, the yachts being sailed in two heats. First heat: 1, Nelson, Mr G Bell; 2, chamrock, Mr T Partington. 2nd heat: 1, Pastime, Mr E Jones: 2, Alice, 31r E Gleave. Third heat: 1 Freak, Mr R Burthem ;2, Win, Mr E Gleave. In the final, Pastime again took first prize; Nelson, 2nd : Freak, 3rd. In the three feet class there were also six entries, and the race was decided in three heats. First heat: 1, Brittannia, Mr Jackson; 2, Stephen, Mr R Williams. Second heat: 1, Griffin, Mr R Woods; 2, Fairy, Mr R Burthetn. Third heat: 1, Albert, Mr G 61eave ; 2, Primrose, Mr A Thompson. In the final, the Griffin was Ist; Albert, 2nd ; Brittannia, 3rd. There were four entries in the big class, which was run off in two heats and a bye, Ada, Mr J Smith, having the bye. First heat : 1, Lily, Mr E Jackson ; 2, Spray, Mr J Ray. Second heat, 1, Thistle, Mr .1 Jackson ; 2, Flying Dutchman, Mr E Baker In the final the Ada won easily, the Lily taking second place, aril the Thistle third. The winners of each class should have sailed off for a copper kettle, presented by Mr Campbell, of the Bowling Green Inn, but, the wind, which had been light all day, died away altogether, and the race had to be postponed.

div.head: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN & NEWTON.

EARLESTOWN TECHNICAL INSTRUCTION CLASSY'S. The following is the result of the examination held in geometrical drawing in connection with the above classes :—John Ashton. William Ball, A G Davies, RA Eaton, James H Eaton. Richard tier- ring, Lewis Johnson, Thomas Ilawdsley, G H Mor- ris, Percy °mend, John Pennington, Joseph Rice, William Savage, Henry Sweetlove, George Wilkin- son, Joseph Worrall, all pass. MASONIC PICNIC FROM NEWTON. On Saturday the members of the Makerfield Lodge, 2155 of Free Masons,had their annual picnic to the Dukeries. The brethren to the number of 40 drove from Newton to Lowton St. Mary's-station where they took train for Worksop. Breakfast was served on arrival,the order afterwards being a drive to Clumber and Thorsley Park, through Sherwood Forest, to Edwinston and Welbeck. Returning to Worksop, dinner was partaken of, and after a very pleasant out, the party made for home reaching Newton about 11-30.

div.head: WELSH CONGREGATIONALISTS, EARLESTOWN.
div.p: WELSH CONGREGATIONALISTS, EARLESTOWN.

The annual picnic in connection with the above body took place on Saturday to Chester. The party numbering 30, left Earlestown at 1-10, reaching Chester about 2 o'clock. A visit to the ancient walls, and Castle was followed by a journey by boat to Eccleston Ferry, where they disembarked and visited Eaton Hall. After inspecting the gardens and parks, they visited the iron bridge. Tea was partaken of at Eccleston Ferry after which, the party returned to Chester, where they visited the Cathedral. The homeward journey was commenced at 9 o'clock, Earlestown being reached at 10-30, after a very enjoyable day. RARLESTOWN ROVERS FOOTBALL CLUB. The presentation of medals won by the players of the above club in the Warrington and District League took place in the Prince of Wales Hotel, on Tuesday evening. Mr. T. Lythgoe, the president of the club, was in the chair and there was a good at- tendance. The Chairman presented the medals to the players and complimented them on their splendid achievements throughout the season. After the presentation,a smoking concert was held songs being rendered by Messrs. Haselden, Gilman Salisbury. Lythgoe, Latham, Crowther, Colquitt and Chadwick; recitation by Mr Martin; and mouth organ solo by Mr Singleton. During the interval refreshments were handed round and a very enjoy- able evening was brought to a close by a vote of thanks to the chairman.

IMPUDENT THEFT AT EARLESTOWN. Two youths, named Albert Mason and Arthur West were charged at the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday with stealing lie. Oid., the money of Alice James, on July Bth. They pleaded guilty.—Florence Taylor, sister of A lice James, complainant, stated that the defendants came into the shop and asked for a copper. They came separately and she refused them both. She saw them pointing towards the till from the window and shortly after she came into the shop and caught Mason with his hands in the till. He ran off with us. 0-Id. and she gave chase. A Mr. Howard eventu- ally caught him. Defendants were each committed for a month's hard labour.—A further charge of damaging a rug value Bs. 2d. in the cell at the Police Station was preferred against them and they again pleaded guilty, being sentenced to 14 days. The sentences were ordered to run concurrently, 60 that prisoners will only be in gaol for one month. 1.0.G.T. HoPH OF EARLESTOWN LODGE No. 1,644. The weekly meeting was held in the Co-operative Hall, Earle-street, on Monday, the programme for the evening being a flower service, the flowers to be sent to sick members and friends. The choir of the Earlestown Mission under the leadership of Mr S Drina, rendered a service of song. " The Mission of the Roses," accompanied by a string band. Mr Kenyon ably presided at the organ. Mr T Dring, who also sang the bass solo" Behold I stand at the door," accompanied at the piano and s'it•ter Mrs Francis feelingly read a lesson on the influence of flowers on the waifs of our large cities. On the motion of Bro. Woods thanks were accorded to the choir for their services, the balance of the collection being given to the choir fund. Arrangements were then made for the visit of the Bolton Claremont Lodge. Mr Dring consented to speak at the ope n air meeting and the invitation to visit the Nil Desperandum Lodge Wigan in September was accepted. NEWTON CONGREGATIONAL SUNDAY SCHOOL. The annual picnic in connection with the elder scholars of the abaye school, together with the teachers, took place on Saturday to Windermere. The party. numbeling about 25, left Newton at 740, and reached Vt, indermere at 11 30. Walking down to the lake they embaiked on the steamer at Ambleside, and sailed up the lake to Bowness, returning to Ambleside on foot and in conveyances. Dinner was partaken of at the latter place, and the next item was a drive to Grasmere, where a short time was spent in looking over the plaee, and a visit to the churchyard and Wordsworth's grave. After tea the remainder of the time was spent in driving, and Windermere was left behind at 6-50, Newton being reached at 9.15, after a thoroughly enjoyable out. The arrangements were carried out by Mr. Law,with the assistance of Mr. D Mc Hardy. _ _ .

ST. JOHN'S CHURCH CHOIR PICNIC. The annual picnic in connection with the above choir took place on Saturday, a number of the Sun- day School teachers accompanying them. Mr. Harrison, the organist, and the Rev. F. Shirtcliffe, curate, had charge of the choir and teachers re- spectively. Leaving Barlestown at 7.13, they journeyed in a reserved carriage to Llangollen, where they arrived shortly after 10 o'clock. They first visited the Old Maid's House and afterwards inspected other places of interest. Dinner was par- taken of at the Bridgend Hotel, after which the party embarked in wagonettes for a visit to the in- teresting portions of the vale. Much disappoint- ment was experienced in consequence of the canal having fallen in which precluded them enjoying what is said to be one of the most interesting items of the visit. Tea was served at 5.45 and the return journey was commenced et 7.25, Earlestown being reached shortly after 10 o'clock. The weather was beautifully fine, and the outing was thoroughly en- joyed.

div.head: FXAMINER, FRI DAY. JULY 21, 199
div.p: THE FXAMINER, FRI DAY. JULY 21, 199

WARRINGTON BOARD OF ' GUARDIANS. A spec;al meeting of this Beard was held in the Board Room at tne Workhouse on Wednesday morning. Mr A J Jolley presided, and there were also present :—Mrs Clay, Mrs EJelsten, Revs T R Matthews, J H Riddette, W El Drummond, Messrs William Hickman. T H Ash- croft, J Biltinge, H Hibbert, H Thornton T B Malkin, S Davies, J W Knowles, R Forshaw, G Pilling, A Jolley. William Houghton, E L Bent, A. Brookes, J Johnson, J Dignum, with Mr J C Sutton (clerk), Mr S Sutton (assistant clerk), Mr Ward (workhouse master). and Mr Wright (superintendent Padgate Schools). THE PRINTING AND STATIONERY CONTRACT. A reference was made to the printing and stationery of the Union, and the Rev. J. H. Riddette expressed the opinion that the newspapers who took the trouble to re- port the proceedings of the Board should bs permitted to do the printing and supply the stationery in turn, providing their charges were reasonable. (Hear, hear.) The CLERK said that two of the papers received no orders at all from the Union. Mr. MALKIN : It is a shame. GIFTS TO THE INMATES. The Workhouse Master acknowledged the following ' gifts Parcel of papers, magazines and flowers from the Rev. Dr. Ewing of St. Barnabas;mazszines from Mr. Pickavance per Mrs. Clay, guardian ; sweets and nuts for children from Mrs. Smethurst of Bewsey-place also from Mr. Ashcroft, guardian,and Dr.G. Braids, medical officer ; oranges for children from Mr. H. Thornton. Mrs. John Fairclough sent tea for the old women and flowers for the wards and Miss Gibson, the cook, gave the children cake for their tea on Walking Day at the Workhouse. Books and papers were also received from the Rev. E. R. Tarbuck, chaplain ; flowers Mrs. Frost, Grapoenhall; Miss Owen, Newholme,Latchlord and Rev. Mr. Ashley, Congregational Church, Lymm. TREAT TO THE SCFIOOh CHILDREN. The SUPERINTENDENT reported that the children were entertained by the Cheshire Lines Cricket Club at War- rington. The children were most liberally supplied with refreshments, and each boy received a prize or present. Large pickets of sweets and nuts were sent for the girls. The Superintendent also reported that Padgate walking day was to take place on July 22ad, and asked that the children be allowed to attend. The request was granted. INCREASE OF LUNATICS. SERIOUS POSITION. The WORKHOUSE MASTER reported that he had had so many violent and rough cases of lunacy and delirium tremeni that it had been necessary to engage the tempor- ary services of extra attendants to look after them until their removal or recovery. The MEDICAL OFFICER reported that there was inPUffi- cient accommodaticn in the House for the iecreasing number of cases of lunacy and delirium tremens. On the 17th he recommended that no further cases be ad- mitted, but the following day a patient was removed to the Haydock Asylum; leaving accommodation for another case in the house. The minutes of the House Committee recommended the appointment of Nurse Alice Bray at a salary of £25. rising to £27 108. at the end of a year's service. The resignation of the cook was accepted. and it was recom- mended that a successor should be appointed at a salary of MO per annum with apartments and rations. It was also recommended that Mary Ellen Vicars be adopted by the Guardians. The CHAIRMAN, in moving the confirmation of the minutes., referred to the increase of cases of lunacy. He said the committee had spent an anxious time in con- sidering the question. The difficulty had been a grave one both to the officere and committee for a long time past. Matters had come to a crisis during the last few days, and it had been necessary to remove two cases to a private asylum at Haydock. The reference in the medical officer's report had compelled them to take steps which up to the present they have endeavoured to avoid. _ _

_ _ Mr. ASHCROFT seconded the confirmation of the minutes. Mr.Horrowron asked for an explanation af the minute which recommended the adoption by the Guardians of Mary Ellen Vickers. The CHSIRMAN said the Guardians would stand in place of the girl's parents. They did not propose to keep her in the house, but would send her to a home. The girl would be under their protection for two years. The minutes were passed. THE:CHAIRMAN AND THE:POOR-LAW CCNFERENCE CLASSIFICATION IN WORKHOUSES. The CHAIRMAN. Vice-Chairman and Clerk were appointed the Board's representatives to attend the annual Poor-Law Conference at Manchester in October. It was stated that the Chairman would read a paper at the Conference on" Differentiation of the treatment of persons in Workhouses." The CLERK said that he had beard papersi read and discussions upon all the subjects to be treated at the 'conference, except that which the Chairman proposed to deal with. He was qnite sure the Chairman would do justice to the subject. (Hear, hear.) It might be deemed advisable for the Chairman to visit one or two workhouses where this classification had existed for ROMA little time, and he would be glad to accompany him. The Chairman would then be abie to deal thoroughly with the question from the point of ViSl9; of its operation in other Unions. (Hear, hear.) The Rev. J. H. RIBDETTE asked if the Board through a deputation had expressed any opinion regarding the present anomaioue state of things by which a vaccina- tion officer was allowed to institute proceedings without reference to the opinions of the Guardians, though the Guardians were liable for all costs. A number of Guar- dians had met to consider the question im conference, and be had ceen looking anxiously to see if Warrington was represented. He had been away, and therefore did not know whether any action hae blen taken. The CHAIRMLN : The que;tion has been raised. The CLERIC said there h d been a meeting in London of representatives of Unions who took a strong view of the question. Perhaps be was responsible for the fact that Warrington was not represented. They had had no experience of difficulties which seemed to have arisen in some other Unions. At one time there was a good deal of discontent at Earleetown, but that seemed to have died away, and for many years they had not had a single complaint, so that they had no interest in the question, and upon his advice perhaps the Board decided not to be represented at the Conference.

STATISTICS FOR THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD. The CLEnx stated that he had received an application from the Local Government Board for a return showing the number of certificates given for succesefnl vaccina- tion from the Ist .June. 1898 to December 30th, 1898, and from January Ist to June 30th, 1899. The figures were as follow : Mr. ilf,lford'a district, 991 and 836 ; Mr Hobaon's district. 320 and 201 ; Mr. Auckland's dis- trict 29 and 32 :Mr. Birchall's district 20 and 28 ' • making totals of 1360 and 897 respectively. He had also furnished a return show- ing the number of paupers of 65 years and upwards on the Ist July last. The number of indoor paupers, ex- chisivn of infirmary patients, 54 males and 21 females ; infirmary 18 malrs 13 females ; outdoor paupers in re- ceipt of Ire medical treatment, 1 male and 2 females ; vagrants in caeual ward, 1 male, 1 female. ALLEGED IMPROPER TREATMENT OF A SICK PAUPER. MR. HIBBERT ASKS FOR AN EXPLANATION. Mr. ITIBBERT said ha had bsen informed that a sick nersoe from Newton named Tom Hitcher), who received an order from Mr. Bowes for admission to the house on Saturday, July B,h. was placed in the tramp ward for two days and died on the following Tuesday in the hospital. It was a case where the man ought to have been takln to the hospital on his admittance. He (Mr. Hibbert) paid the man's fare to Warrington and knew that he was ill at the time. Ho thought it was a case that ought to be investigated. The CHAIRMAN asked whether it was the wish of the Board that the matter should be gone into now or by the House Commitee at its next meeting. The Board decided to investigate the matter at once. Mr. PILLING said he had been looking at the books of the institution and he found an entry that on July Bth, Hitchen was admitted to the house. It was therefore clear that the man was not placed in the tramp ward. Mr. WARD (in answer to questions by Mr. Forshaw) said the man was admitted to the receiving ward on the date named. He would remain there until he had been examined by the doctor. Mr. BOWES (relieving officer for the Newton District) stated that Hitchie came to him for an order to the Workhouse stating that he didn't feel so %ell and in- tended to stop in for about a week. Mr. ASHCROFT He came here perhaps to get away front drink ? Mr. HIBBERT : He had had no drink for two or three weeks previously. Rev. T. R. MiarrnEws : Had he been under medical treatment in Newton ? Mr. BOWES: No. Mr. Donsme, an attendant at the Workhouse was then called into the room and questioned by the Chairman. Tbe CHAIRMAN : Wore you in charge of the porter's lodee en the Bth July? Mr. DOBSON : Yes. The CHAIRMAN: Do you remember a man coming from Newton named Hitchin with an order from the re- lieving officer? Mr. DOBSON : Yes I do. The CHAIRMAN: Do you remember anything about the man's appearance or his statement at the time? Mr. DOBSON : I asked him if he wag poorly, and he said he didn't feel so well. I nut him in the receiving ward where he was bathed and changed. He slept in the receiving ward that night. The CMAIRMAN : Did he make any complaint that he wag unwell ? Mr. KNowLss Anyone would have known that from his statement. The Rev. J. H. RIDDETTE : How long is a person kept in the receivine ward ? The CHAIRMAN: It all depends on circumstances. If there is any suspicion of infectious;disease be is removed

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.

ST. HELENS VOLUNTEERS AND THE BISLEY COMPETITfONS. The iolto wing members of the 2ad Volunteer Battalion South Lencashire Regiment, whose headquarters are at St. Helens, have journeyed to Bisley to take part in the Queen's and other shooting contests :—Captain F white, Lieutenant F J West, Sergeant-Instructor Butler,Colour- Sergeant-Instructor Bagley, Sergeants G Junor, W Milligan. and D Gamble Lance-Sergeant R Norbury, Corporals W Glover, T Lockie, and R M'Gill, and Private E Nicholson. MESSRS. BEECHAM AND THEIR WORIEPEOPLE. The annual excursion provided by Messrs. Beecham and Son, of St. Helens, the well-known pill makers.was held on Saturday, when about 120 of the employes. with their wives, journeyed to Llandudno. The party, accom- panied by Mr. W. Moss,works manager, Mr. E. Glover, and Mr. C. T. Scrymgeour were conveyed in special saloon carriages attached to the 6 55 a.m. train, and on their arrival at Chester they were supplied in the saloons with a substantial breakfast. At Llandudno they were joined by Mr. C. Rcre Ed, general manager for the firm, and the Grosvenor Restaurant was made the head- quarters for the day. Dinner and tea were served there, and the day's arrangements included free admission to the pier and other attractions. The whole of the ex- penses were defrayed by the firm, and the workpeole, in addition, received their day's wages. A Cow IN A DWELLING-HOUSE AT ST. HELENS. A somewhat remarkable incident was witnessed in Bickerstaff-street, St. Helens, on Friday night. Some cows were being driven alooe, the street, when one of the animals made a suMen dash for the open door of the dwelling house. No. 42,occupied by a Mr. Richardson. The cow walked down the lobby, and as its approach was noticed, the occupants, who were naturally greatly alarmed, closed the door leading into the kitchen. The cow continued its course to about half way up the stairs, facing the lobby, where it stuck fast for a time. Several men quickly followed the animal, which after some little trouble was released and "backed " down the stairs and into the street, to the great relief of the occupants of the house. Fortunately no damage was done by the cow's unwelcome intrusion. THE ELECTRIC TRAMWAYS AT ST. HELENS. The Board of Trade inspection of the sections of the S. Helens and District Tramways, which have been fitted up for electric traction, was made on Wednes- day, and as soon as the official sanction has been ob- tained the Corporation will introduce a regular and vastly improved service. The sections completed up to the present are those to Prescot and Denton's Green,aod the work upon other lines is being rapidly proceeded with. Under the powers recently obtained from Parlia- ment the St. Helens Corporation are now urging for- ward the extensions of the tramway system at Haydock at Parr, at Prescot, and at Peasley Cross, and St. Helens Junction. A c-annaencement of the work at Haydock was made on Monday, the contract for that portion having been secured by Messrs. Hughes and Stirling, of Liverpool. Messrs. R. W. and A. Heaton, of St. Helens, have obtained contracts for the work on the other sec- tions. A SINGULAR DISAPPEARANCE FROM ST. HELENS. In the Chancery of Lancashire, sitting at St. George's Hall, Liverpool, on Monday. Vice-Chancellor Hall heard an application in the action Foster v. Power, adjourned for a report by the registrar. Mr. Harold Mather applied that the court would declare Sarah Swire to have died unmarried before the age of 21 years. In July. 1876, when aged eight years, she disappeared from St. Plelens, and her father, William Swire, never heard of her again. He died in 1881, leaving his daughter a share of about £7OO in his estate should she be alive. Since the case was before the court the registrar bad advertised in various newspapers, but no news arrived concerning the missing girl, and it was presumed she had died.—Mr. R. Law- rence said it was for the benefit of the youngest beneficiaire that the money should be paid over.—His Honour made the required order, declaring that Sarah Swire had died before attaining her majority.

div.head: PENKETH.
div.p: PENKETH.

MEETING OF THE PARISH COUNCIL.—The quarterly meeting of the Penketh Parish Council was held in the Day Star Institute on Monday evening. Mr. Roisert Garnett presided, and there were alse present Dr. T. A. Murray, Mr. John Dignum, and Mr. E. Foster (clerk).— Dr. Murray said an offer had been made to them for the use of the Star Institute as a mortuary, and he thought if they let the place they would have to let the autho- rities know that classes were held there in the winter.—The Clerk was instructed to ad- vise the Park Company and the police.—Mr. Dignum said that a complaint had ben made to him about carts running on to the footpath at the corner of Heath-read and Cemetery-road. It was thought that the Surveyor should place a small curb stone at the corner, but that would be a matter for the district Council.—The Chairman: They should put an old cannon there upside down. (Laughter.)—Dr. Murray : This is worth bringing forward at the Dis- trict Council meeting.—The Chairman : The corner is dangerous and would be more dangerous if a curbstone were put there. The only thing is to erect a post of some kind.—Dr. Murray said that would be dangerous at night.—lt was decided that Mr. Dignum should men- tion the matter at the District Council meeting..--Mr. Dignurn asked if anything could be done to improve the lighting of the villae.e. A short discussion followed,and Mr. Dignum was asked to submit a resolution to the next meeting.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CITURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CITURCHES.

GOSPEL HALL, FORSTER-STREET. On Sunday night, Mr. Joseph Dale, of Knutsford, Preached on "The Apostle Paul" (Acts 9). He said Paul, even before his conversion, was a pattern man, eons could lay a finger upon his life, and in persecuting the Christian, he really believed he was doing God's ser- vice. He was no hypocrite. His purnose was to gain Heaven by his own goad works, and if it had been nos- sible,none more likely than he to have succeeded. In the midst of this work Christ met him and found out that all his works counted for nothing, Christ having done the work which fits man for Heaven. The Christian does not work for salvation, but because he has salva- tion. When Paul vras converted God entrusted him with the Gospel; which he in turn handed down to faithfal men to spread the news of a free salvation. That salvation is still offered to men and women, and will be so while the day of grace lingers. If that day were to Close the case of the unsaved would be hopeless. It was therefore wise to settle the matter now. ELLESMERE-STREET WE'ILEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.

Successful anniversary services in connection with the Ellesmere-street Wes'evan Sunday school were held in the Bold-street Wesleyan Church on Sunday. in the afternoon a musical service took place. Mr. W. Silcock presided, and addressed a few encouraging, words to the children, speaking of the influence they could use for good. What grand inetitutions their Snnday Schools would be if all the children who attended them became good women and brave and self-denying men. During the service solos were efficiently renderer], and Miss G Shaw Green ably recited " Silence in Amen Corner." Miss Hannah Brough sang the " Psalm of Life," Mrs Williams" The Chorieer "and Mr. Gough " Dawning Light." At the evening service the soloists were Miss Hannah Broug,h and Mr. Levi Richardson. Special hymns were sung by the children, who were assisted by the choir, at both services. There were large congrega- tions. Collections were taken in aid of the Ellesmere- street Sunday School funds. The Rev. H. G. Roberts M.A. was the preacher for the occasion.

div.head: ROWING REGATTA AT HOWLEY QUAY.
div.p: ROWING REGATTA AT HOWLEY QUAY.

On Saturday a rowing regatta, 'organised by Mr. George Platt, of the Rowley Boat Rouse, was com- pleted in the Presence of between 300 to 400 spec- tators The first and second rounds were rowed on Saturday, the Bth July, and the third round, semi- final, and :final on Saturday. The race was tor single pair oared skiffs, and the prizes were first, marble clock, and second, gold medal. There were 22 competitor,. The draw for the first round re- sulted in the fnllowing being drawn tovether. the first named in each instance being the winner of their respective heats, viz, Messrs J T Bailey v J Strange, W Morgan. v T Clifford. G Allen, v 3 P Ditchfield, v W Ditchfield,W Dobson, v B Pluropton, W Spencer v C Drinkivater, and W Bancroft v W Clifford. Messrs J Davenport,J Ditch- field, E Tynan,C Phillins,W Robinson, F Simcock,W Aurgess, I Burst. and W Floyd receiving byes, and therefore entering the second round without a con- test. The draw for the second round resulted as follows Davenport v J Hurst, J Ditchfield v W Floyd, C illip v E Tynan, W Morgan v W Rob- inson, W Dobson v F Simcock. T Bailey v W Ban- croft, G Allen v W Spencer, P Ditchfield v W Bur- gess. The third round was as follows :—W Morgan v C Phillips, P Ditchfield v G Allen, J Davenport v J T Bailey, J Ditchfield v W Dobson, semi-final, W Morgan v J Davenport; and P Ditchfield v J Ditch- field, and final, W Morgan, beat P Ditch field. The distance was about 900 yards. Some of the beats had very close finishes, notably those of Morgan and Robinson in the second round. Bailey and Davenport in the third round, and the Brothers Ditchfield in the semi-final. The times were very even, averaging about five minutes until towards the semi-final, when the rowing very perceptably increased, the time for the final being 4min. 22sec. The prizes were banded to the winners at the con- clusion of the racing. Messrs T and W Whittle, W Stringer, F T Garnett, and J G Chappell, officiated as starters and judges.

immediately. The Rev. J. g —IDDETTE : I simply want to know if the man was subjected to the ordinary procedure ? The CHAIRMAN : I believe he was. Mr. WARD . The ordinary procedure is that when a person is admitted to the receiving ward, he is bathed, and receives a change of clothing. He then waits there until the medical officer sees him, and determines to which part of the house the person must go to. Mr. KNOWLES: It a man said that his reason for eoneing into the Workhouse was that he wasn't so well, which is a common Lancashire expression for illness, do you think it part of 'your duty or of your deputy's to allow him to be bathed ? The CHAIRMAN : It is part of the duties in the hos- pital. Mr. KNOWLES : You might kill a man by such conduct in certain cases of illness. The Cattlemen : You can ask the officer whether the man raised any objections. Mr. KNOWLES : He would think it was the usual thing lad would obey orders. Before anythieg is done to a sick man be ought te be seen by a doctor. To bathe a man of that kind is rashness and ignorance. The CHAIRMAN said he would be glad if members would retrain from making rash expressions before they were aware of the facts. Mr. KNOWLES: The porter has stated that the man was put in a bath and I think it was a most improper thing to do. Rev. J. H. lIIDDETTE said the circumstances seemed to suggest the desirability of teleptsonic communicae:ioa with the Medical Officer until such times as they had a resident medical officer. He quite agreed that no opinion should be expressed until the whole case was before them. The CHAIRMAN said they had Mr. Bow& distinct • statement that the man had not been under medical treatment. They had no right to assume that the man was unwell. Mr. Honszae said the man had been medically at- tended but not for some weeks prior to his admission to the Workhouse. The CHAIRMAN :71 hope we are not going to challenge any officer's statement without good authority. Mr. PILLING moved that the matter be referred to the House Committee. The Chetereeer : The Board has decided to investi- gate the matter now. Mr. FORSHAW (to Mr. DobSatl) How long was the man in the receiving ward? Mr. DOBSON . I took him to the hospital on Sunday morning. He slept in the receiving ward one night. Mr. FORSHAW : Where did he die? Mr. DonsoN : In the heseital. Mr. ASEICROFT : When did the doctor see him? Mr. Donsme On Sunday morning. Mr. HICKMAN : Mr. flitibert's statement is not cor- rect then. The CHAIRMAN: Whenever there is any appearanc of serious illness :the doctor is sent for, and whatever time his services are needed, without the slightest hesi- tation he always comes. The Rev. J. H. KIDDETTE : If the man had died from pneumonia there is no doubt the bath would accelerate his death. Mr. HIBBERT : He had heart disease. Mr. THORNTON : What was the ceetified Cause of death ? The CHAIRMAN : Pneumonia. It would be highly improper to condemn any officer of having done any- thing wrong on the evidence before us. Mr. CLARE : It is the system which is condemned. The CHAIRMAN : If anyone is prepared to suggest a better one the House Committee will be pleased to con- sider it. The Rev. J. H. BIDDETTE said he did not think any officer was to blame but the system was wrong which could allow such a thing to happen. He had pleaded several times for some means of immediate communica- tion with the Medical Officer. He should like to see a resident Medical Officer, but there ought to be some means of communicating with the Medical Officer at once when there was a case needing his attention. It would be unwise to censure the porter or master. They knew what a disease pneumonia was, and it was a dangerous thing to do what had been done in this case, but still anyone of them might have committed the same error. The CLERIC said Mr. Shearer would read an extract from a letter he had received from the deceased man's son. Mr. SHEARER said the son wrote thanking everyone in connection with the Workhouse for the care and kind- ness shown to his father whilst there. (Hear, hear.) The Rev J. H. RIDDETTE: That seems to end the case except any recommendation it may be wise to make. Mr. BENT thought the press ought to be asked to leave out the discussion. ThR CHAIRMAN said the Board could leave the reporters to we their discretion in the matter. The feeline of the B,ard seemed to be quite unanimous that the 'flitter should be dealt with immediately. No one knew better than himself the futility as a general rule of a large body dealing with a delicate question of that kind. On several occasions he (the Chairman) had had to call Mr. Hibbert to order and there had been an opinion that there was some personal feeling between them. There was nothing of the kind and he hoped Mr. Hibbert realised that he had had fair play and the case investi- gated as fully as possible. There was nothing to justify the remarks of Ur. Knowles. The officers appeared to have dealt with the case according to the rules laid down. No blame attached to any officer, and the sug- gestion that they should postpone their bathing of in- mates was simply childish. What some people did want was a bath. Mr. lIIBIERT thought that when an inmate died the information should be conveyed to friends. He did sot hear that the man was dead until some days afterwards. Mr. WARD said he sent word to the man's son as to the illness and also as tn the death. Mr. BROOKS said he was glad to know that the man was not treated in the tramp ward but in accordance with the regulatioes of the helm. The subject then dropped, and the Board rose soon afterwards.

TEE SEEITICE IN HILL CLIFFE GRAVEYARD.—Last Sun- day evening was the best attended of these open air services since they have been started, and the evening was the most ideal yet enjoyed, hence the attendance was larger and the enjoyment was greater. In the ab- sence of the pastor (who crag called away suddenly to supply an anniversary emergency), the Rev John Aldis (Little Leigh) preached an excellent sermon on John iii. H. The singing was better, for a new instrument had been secure, and altogether the service was of a most pleasing and hearty character.

EXAMINATION OF PUPIL TEACHERS.

The class list ot the examination in religious know- leige of pupil teachers in elementary schools within the diocese of Liverpool. which was held on June 17, under the auspices of the Diocesan Board of Education and School Society has just been issued by the diocesan inspeetor. COVENTRY CHIEF CON STABLESHIP .-A WAR-
RINGTON CANDIDATE.

At a meeting of the Watch Committee of the Coventry Corporation thirty-eight applications for the post of chief constable, vacant by the resigna- tion of Mr. A. Gray, were considered. The Mayor (Dr. Webb Fowler, presided at the meeting, and the number of applicants was reduced to seven, to be subsequently further reduced by the committee. The seven selected were : Inspector Arrow, of Scotland Yard, London; Inspector Shelley, of the Coventry police force; Chief-clerk Thompson, of Nottingham; Chief-inspector Charsley, of Birming- ham ; Chief-constable Coleman, of Truro; Chief- constable Sterling, of Newcastle-under-Lynn; and Chief Inspector Phillips, of Warrington.

The usual Sunday and .N.l.onday meetings in con- nection with the Spiritualist Society were addressei by Miss Jones, of Liverpool, each address being fol- lowed by clairvoyance and psychometric readings.

div.head: CATTLE AND HORSE FAIRS" AT WARRINGTON
div.p: CATTLE AND HORSE FAIRS" AT WARRINGTON

The cattle fair was held on Monday en the ground behind the Blue Coat School. There was a compara- tively poor market, but a fair number of much cows were sold and exchanged. The horse fair took place on Tuesday, when there was a poor show, but some fair prices were realised.

John Tearney, 20, Mausfield-street, Manchester, was taking a horse from Warrington to Manchester on Tuesday evening, when the animal threw him, and he was rather seriously bruised about the legs and head. He was taken to the Infirmary and de- tained.

div.head: THELWALL PARISH COUNCIL.
div.p: THELWALL PARISH COUNCIL.

A meeting of this Council was fixed for Monday evening, but the only members present were Mr. Norman Taylor (chairman), and Mr J Tuck, with Mr. 1-1 Roebuck (for Mr W E Cooke) (clerk). After waiting for half an hnur, the Chairman adjourned the meeting for a fortnight. The business was correspondence relative to the new county rate basis, the village footpath, and the drain and road in Vtilste-lane. BAND OF BOPE OPEN-AIR RALLY.

Under the auspices of the Warrington and Dis- trict Band of Hope Union an open-air rally was held on Saturday on the new fair ground, off Orford- lane. The Rev. E. T. Reed presided,and Mr. Taylor, podc-.8 court missionary, gave an excellent address. Miss Ball and Miss Hill contributed recitations,and solos were given by Mr. William Woods and Mr. C. Nurse. The choir rendered several choruses very effectively.

div.p: SINGULAR bEA.TII. AT ACTON 13RIDGR.

On Thursday afternoon Mr. Worsley,Coroner, con- ducted an inquiry at Acton Bridge, near Warring- ton, into the circumstances attending the death of a farm labourer named Martin Gam, aged fifty,who was found dead in a barn on Tuesday morning. The evidence showed that on Monday evening,when coming from a hayfield, be met a man named Gerrard. He commenced sparring in a jocular way, and slipped over a piece of iron, his head becoming impaled on the raiiings. Verdict, "Death from syncope due to loss of blood." THE LATE Mn CHARLES DEWHIIRST._ .

In hi;-s-er;Co-n-oi--eut-JaTe-v-e-ning, at the Parish Church, the Rector indirectly alluded to the death from dysentery, ofiMr. Charles:Dewhurst, R.N. (son of Ur. John Dewhurst, headmaster of the National Schools, Church-street), which occurred in hospital on the East Coast of Africa, on July 10th. Canon Willis observed that all the congregation would sympathize with the bereaved family. At the conclusion of the service the Dead March in "Saul" was played by the organist, Mr. W. S. Woods. TEMPERANCE HALL, LATCHFORD. The weekly meeting of the Latchford Good Ternolars was held in the above hall on Monday evening, Councillot. Ellison presiding. Thera was a good attendance. It was decided to forward a let- ter of sympathy to one of the members of the Order who is under treatment in the Manchester Infirm- ary. The programme of the evening was "Ques- tions." The questions had reference to the manage- ment and conduct of the Good Templar Order, and were of an entertaining And instructive character

div.head: SWARM OF BEE'S IN MA.RXET-STREET..
div.p: A SWARM OF BEE'S IN MA.RXET-STREET..

There was a novel sight in Market-street on fuesday morning. A swarm of over 2,000 Chehire bees came from the direction of Horsemarket- street, and settled on the sunshade in front of Messrs Eastman's Limited, butcher's shop. Mr. Birch, market-gardener and florist, obtained a hive, and after some difficulty succeeded in hand- ling the queen bee. lie placed her in the hive and the swarm followed shortly afterwards. 't he singu- lar scene attracted a large crowd, and the capture of the bees V1£1,9 witnessed with great interest.

THE PRISON VAN:IN 'COLLISION. An accident happened to Miss Crosfield, daughterof Mr. John Crosfield, J.P., of Walton Lea, on Monday afternoon. She and her sister were driving into town in a trap, when on reaching Bridge-foot a collision took place with the prison van, which was being driven to Bank Quay Station by a man named Joseph Han- son. Miss Crosfield was thrown out of the trap into the road, and it was thought had sustained serious injuries. She was taken into Mr. Boothroyd's music shop and Dr. Langdale was summoned. He found that Miss Crosfield was fortunately only slightly bruised and shaken,and allowed her to be conveyed home in a cab. PICNICS TO FOUTHPORT. On Saturday the members of the choir of All Saints' Mission, tsewsey-road,and a few friends had a trip to Southport. leaving at 9.30 a.m. and re- turning at 9 p.m. They were accompanied by Mies Westwell, mission lady, and Mr. Sudlow, superin- tendent of the Sunday school. Dinner and tea were provided at Thorpe's restaurant. On Monday those attending St. Paul's Mothers' Meetings also went to Southport,being accompanied by the Vicar and Mrs. Tarbuck, Miss Westwell, and Mr. and Mrs. Chantry. By the kindness of the Rev. H. S. Hope, vicar of Holy Trinity Church,one of the schools was placed at the disposal of the party for tea. The weather being favourable each day, the visits to Southport were thoroughly enjoyed. SUICIDE OF A RETIRED WARRINGTON MILITARY OFFICER AT EA.STHAM.

At the Eastham Ferry Hotel, on Wednesday even- ing, Mr. J. C. Bate, coroner for West Cheshire, held an inquest on the body of George Evan, fifty-four years of age, a retired military officer, whose address was 25, Gorsey-lane, Warrington. The evidence showed that on Thursday last deceased disappeared from the Eastham Ferry Hotel, where he had been staying for some time previously, and his body was discovered on Wednesday by Police-Constable Dut- ton in the Ship Canal at Eastham. Several articles of his attire had been found on the canal bank on the day of his disappearance, and it now transpired ;bat he had left behind him a letter in which he sianified his intention of committing suicide. The jury found a verdict of "Suicide whilst temporarily insane." . _ .

The ai—nu—al7.itee-t-i4 of the subscribers to the Daresbury nurse fund took place in the Sessions Room, on Monday evening, the Vicar presiding, There were present :—Mrs Clark, Mrs White, Mrs Woods, Mrs Litton; and Messrs John White, Wynne Jones, and J Wright. Mr. Wynne Jones, the treasurer, submitted the statement of accounts, which was approved. For several years two nurs- ing associations have been in existence in the parish, but recently an amalgamation took place and the Daresbury Rural District Nurse Association was formed, the following ladies and gentlemen forming the committee :—President, liev H T Clark; vice-presidents, Mrs W C Jones (Elms) and Mrs Wynne Jones; committee, Mrs Clark, Mrs John White, Mrs Herbert Woods, Mrs Z Armitage, Mrs Webb, and Mies B Dutton; Mrs Litton, hon. secre- tary, and Mr. H. Congreve (hon. treasurer.) The services of Nurse Wallace, from the Queen's Nursing Institution, has been engaged, and she will shortly enter upon her duties. TERRIBLE TRAGEDY IN LONDON. A tmible crime is reported from Walworth, London, where a man yesterday moraing, in the absence of his wife, murdered his two children, and afterwards cut his own throat. The ma 1 was still alive when dis- covered.
A later account states that the man who murdered his two children at Walworti is Robert Ward, a bricklayer, aged 27. He had beeu drinking for a week.

WILD PARROTS IN CHESHIRE. It is exceedingly rare that tropical birds of any species are found flying in this country, but during the past fortnight three Amazon parrots have been living about in the neighbourhood of BarrAton and Little Leigh, near Northwich. The birds have played havoc with unripe fruli;, pulling it off the trees, and throwing it to the ground. One has been caught, and another shot,whilst committing its depredations, the third being still at large.

- DEATHS THROUGH THE HEAT. George Petchey, 52, labourer, and Walter Ryley, 32, Watelayer, died suddenly in So -th Essex on Wednesday. Their deaths are attributed to the great heat. THE CONDITION OF BRIGGS. There is no change to report in the COrlditiOrl of Briggs. It was stated upon inquiry that sense weeks must elapse before any material improvement can take place. DEGREES FOR EMINENT MEN. Glasgow University yesterday conferred degrees upen various eminent persons. The best known were Sir Henry Irving and Col. Hector Macdonald, recipients of the degree of L.L Xi. Each received an ovation, and the students sang "For he's a jolly good fellow," and " Soldiers of the Queen." LANCASHIRE COUNTY COUNCIL. APPOINTMENT OF CLERK. Yesterday the Standing Joint Committee of Lanca- shire appointed Mr. Harcourt E. Clare, Town Clerk of Liverpool, to the office of Clerk of the Peace for Lanca- shire. The office carries with it the clerkship of the Lancashire County ECounril and the county solicitorship and is worth £3,000 per annunt. LATEST LOCAL WEATHER FORECAST. The following forecast of the weather for the ensuing twenty-four hours in the north-west of Englaxd was issued at the Meteorological Office at three o'clock yes- terday afternoon : Varying north-easterly breezes, light ; fine. div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

VOLUNTEERS..—We understand that Mr.W. G. Linaker, of Frodsham, has been gazetted as a 2nd lieutenant of the 2ed Earl Chester's Battalion Cheshire Regiment, Volunteer Rifles. Mr. Linaker, we feel sure, will do much to stimulate the volunteer movement. SUNDAY SCHOOL ANNIVERSARY.—TWO sermons Were preached in the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Frodshani, on Sunday, by the new Paetor,the Rev. A. K. Kynaston, special hymns and anthems being tastefully rendered by the choir. Mr. Jame. Hough was ,at the organ. In the afternoon a miscellaneous service was conducted, presided over by Mr. Kynaston, at which vockl and in- strumental music was rendered and recitations contri- buted. The offertories for the day realised £l6. FRODSHAM PAROCHIAL COMMITTRE.—At the monthly meeting of the Frodsham Parochial Committee, on Fri- day evening Mr. Charles E. Linaker presiding. the Clerk, Mr. G. F Ashton. reported that Messrs. Cross. ey Brothers had givan the revisit° guarantee for the proper working of the gas pumping engine. The Chair. man referred to tho old grievance which had arisen owing to the hot weather, namely, the disagreeable stench emanating from the bones being discharged ora the railway siding. He thought something ought to be done to remedy the nuisance. It was resolved that the attention of the railway company be again called to the matter.—From the report of the Water Committee it appeared that the Frodsham Gas and Water Co., bad applied fur terms whereby the new gasometer could be filled with water from the water mains to the extent of 600,000 gallons, and it has been decided that is. per thousand gallons be charged, the Gas Company to laY all pipes needful for the purpose.—The Water Corn. mittee also reported that the water engineer had applied for an increase of salary and that this matter had beeo referred to the Parochial Committee. It was resolved that the salary of Mr. Rodgers, the water engineer, be increased from 28s. to 309. per week and that when the Frodsham Lordship Water Scheme is completed the matter he again considered.—' The Surveyor produced a plan showing the plan of cCt. tam n semi-detached residences it was proposed to erect on land opposite to South Bank, Frodsham, belonging to Mr W E Thornton, but as the plan did not show * secondary street 20 feet wide in accordance with tke bylaws in force he considered that it should not be ap- proved. The Chairman suggested that by reducing the number of houses it would be possible to give a space of 20 feet between each pair of houses, Mr. Kydd moved, and Mr. P. Booth seconded, that. the plan submitted be approved, providing Mr. Thornton Was willing to pro. vide a space of not less than 20 feet between each block of building. Mr. Earlain its. wed that the plan be not appreved,the same not being in accordance with the by. laws. In order to test the meeting. Mr. Williams seconded the amendment,and on its being put to the meeting two voted in favour, and nine against, whereupon the pro- position was declared carried.

WESLEYAN SUNDAY SCHOOL. —OD MOD iay afternoon tbe scholars connected with the Weston Wesleyan Sundar School journeyed to Overton Hill in wagonettes. At the time of starting, about eleven o'clock,there was a record number present. On arrival at the hills dinner WO served, and in. the afternoon the scholars enjoyed nail- selves in various ways, some rambling over the heightSt while others found recreation in games and pastimee• This exercise put a keen edge oc the appetite, and a sub' stantial tea was not the least item in the programme. The party subsequently embarked on the return journei Runcorn being reached about six o'clock. The weatblo was beautifully fine and proved an important factor 0 the success of the proce,dings.

WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH OF WARRINGTON. Week Ending Saturday Bth July, 1899. During the week the following births and deaths were registered : Births. Deaths. Warrington Registration District 51 25 The excess of births over deaths was 26. The Birth Rate was equal to 41 6 per 1,000. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 204 per 1,000, against 221 the average of the previous 4 weeks, and against 14.08 the corresponding period of last year. The death- rate from the seven chief zvmotic diseases was equal to 3.2 per 1,000. against 6.4 the average rate of the previous 4 weeks, and against nil the corresponding period of 1898. The ages of mortality were- -0-1 1-5 5-15 15-25 25-65 65 tip. 12 2 4 6 1 25 The deaths included 2 from scarlet fever, 3 from phthisis, 2 from lung diseases, 2 whoopingcough 2 from rheumatic fever, 1 from injuries, 13 from all other causes. The following cases of Infectious Disease have been reported during the week :—Scarlet fever 15 cases, erysipelas 1 case. Total number of patients in hospital week ending Bth July, 47. METEOROLOGY—The mean temperature was 59.7 Fab., and therefore about the same as preceding week. The maximum temperature 74 F., was recorded on the 6th inst., and the minimum temperature 42 F., on the 4th inst. The Rainfall measured 29 inch. The general direc- tion was N. JOHN H. GORNALL, Medical Officer of Health.
